speechtext:
am very happy to have the privilege of taking part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, particularly at the present time when I am given the opportunity of supporting the subamendment which was so capably presented to this house last Thursday by my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw). This subamendment criticized the government for failing to take effective action to stop the continuous rise in the cost of living; secondly, the failure of the government to lay down and follow policies under which the Canadian farmers and other primary producers can enjoy an equitable share of the prosperity

The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith which Canada can achieve; thirdly, the failure of the government to bring old age pensions and other social security payments into line with the present cost of living.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with a few of the many problems which are confronting men and women engaged in our basic industry, agriculture, and to suggest to the government a few steps which, if the government is truly interested in the wellbeing of this industry, can be taken to relieve the situation in which farmers across Canada now find themselves. Since coming down here we have been made very conscious of the fact we are going to ask the people across Canada very soon to again choose the government they wish to manage the affairs of our great country for another four or five years. Since that is the case, now is the time for each and every one of us in this house to do a little reflecting. We should ask ourselves a few very simple questions such as these: Have we in the past years done our best to serve our constituents and the people across Canada as they deserve to be served? Have we seen to it that all phases of our economy have been fairly treated or have we permitted some sectors of our economy to suffer?
As to the last question, Mr. Speaker, we in this group feel that many segments of our economy have been badly treated. It is interesting to read the glowing accounts of our national prosperity but it is very difficult to reconcile this rosy picture with the true state of affairs found in the agricultural industry, especially when we find approximately 18 per cent of the people who are engaged in agriculture in Canada receiving less than 7 per cent of the national income. However, we cannot find any evidence in the speech from the throne that it is the intention of the present government to do anything about this situation. It is true that this matter has been causing great concern throughout Canada. In fact, the supporters of the present government, the delegates who attended the Alberta Liberal association convention at Calgary in November of last year, expressed their dissatisfaction with the federal agriculture policy, if it could be called a policy, which has been followed over the years. According to press reports this convention asked for a system of parity prices on farm products, and also urged the government towards greater efforts to find markets for our grain and other agriculture products.
This convention passed a resolution urging the government to provide long-term loans to young farmers. Another resolution which was passed at this particular convention


deals with the equalization of floor prices for hogs as between the eastern and Pacific coast markets. I am given to understand that a good percentage of the delegates attending the convention represented the agriculture industry of Alberta and one delegate used these words in describing his position. "Farmers are clinched; they cannot move. The government tells us we are prospering but everyone is in debt." In order to prove my statement that these delegates who are supporting the Liberal party are concerned and are unhappy about the situation as it now exists may I cite the fact they said "that something must be done about agriculture policy if we wish to elect Liberal members in the west".
Now, Mr. Speaker, these requests I have mentioned have been a part of the agriculture program of the Social Credit party down through the years. Even though we have advocated these policies in this house, the government has not seen fit to do anything about them. Last summer, for example, to give you one illustration, we received the assurance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that after the end of the crop year, July 31, he would see to it that attempts would be made to ensure that those points in the west which were on a low quota basis would be given a preference in the new crop year. I wish to be fair in this matter. I do not wish to blame the Canadian wheat board at all for the chaotic conditions that exist in the marketing of wheat in the west. Even though the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is reported to have made this statement while attending a meeting in southern Alberta: that the Canadian wheat board was the sole control of the marketing of wheat I am not prepared to accept that statement. The Minister of Agriculture knows full well that the Canadian wheat board can market our wheat only within the confines of the faulty marketing policies of the present Liberal government and the financial policies adopted by the government as well.
Last summer we had the privilege of sitting in on the hearings of the agricultural committee at which the Canadian Pacific Railway was in attendance. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Pacific Railway must stand condemned for a part of the situation which now exists on the western prairies as far as grain marketing is concerned. I feel that the Canadian Pacific Railway deliberately failed to co-operate last spring with the then transport controller. I can find little evidence, Mr. Speaker, that the same railway has tried very seriously to do anything about relieving the

situation that is found on the Canadian Pacific lines in western Canada at the present time.
I have followed the marketing of grain in my riding very closely and I have found many points which were on a 5-bushel quota had not completed their 2-bushel quota at the end of the crop year, July 31, 1956. On the other hand, I know of points in western Canada which were on an 8-bushel quota on July 31 of last year and have now achieved a completed 3-bushel quota. I have been in constant touch with the Canadian wheat board with regard to this situation, since it affects farmers in my riding, and I just wish to read briefly from a letter which I received in November from a leading official of the Canadian wheat board. He had this to say:
I would point out that both railways have materially increased their car supply in the shipping of grain during the period from August 1 up to present. From August 1 to October 31, the C.P.R. has supplied 43,830 cars as compared to 28,415 last year; the C.N.R. has supplied 41,598 cars as compared to 29,278 last year. However, notwithstanding the fact that the C.P.R. have increased their supply by approximately 15,000, the C.N.R. have increased their cars by approximately 12,000, but the total number of cars supplied by each road is just about equal when you take into consideration that about 57 per cent of the grain that we have for shipment is located on the C.P.R., with about 43 per cent on the C.N.R. You will appreciate that, as long as the C.N.R. continues to match the C.P.R. supply the stations on the C.N.R. will be in better shape than those on the C.P.R.
In other words, just as long as this government refuses to appoint a new transport controller with the power to direct orderly and equitable marketing of grain in the west this situation will continue and the farmers living along the C.P.R. lines will continue to be discriminated against.
I know that some attempts have been made to justify this situation. Several reasons have been advanced. Most of the reasons which have been advanced have been decidedly weak. Perhaps one of the most prevalent reasons is the need of wheat of a particular quality; that shipping orders are given for a certain grade of wheat. That argument does not stand up when you look at two points not more than 10 miles apart. The wheat marketed at these two points is in most instances of the same quality and grade. Therefore, that argument must necessarily fall down.
In closing this matter, Mr. Speaker, may I say I do feel that the government should do something immediately to see that the Canadian Pacific Railway takes immediate steps to put into the west the same percentage of cars as the C.N.R. They should do something about trying to catch up with the manmade lapse of six weeks last spring. As I pointed out a moment or so ago, the situation
The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith
in the west continues to be serious. In the west low quotas mean that the farmers are unable to market their grain. It means that they are unable to get cash money to pay their taxes and to do other things. We are told that one of the reasons that there is such a glut of wheat in the west is that there is a surplus of grain throughout the world. At this time I wish to refer to a short article which is entitled, "How Big Is The Surplus?" It deals with the surplus of wheat as it exists in the world today and reads as follows:
The present large stocks of wheat are a serious impediment to the ready marketing of new production. They are regarded gloomily by governments, farmers and business people in the export countries. The Canadian Bank of Commerce recently termed the wheat carryover as "astronomical".
There is no doubt that under our pattern of trade and distribution the situation is serious but the volume is inclined to impress us beyond its real proportions. We see the 11 billion bushel world carryover as almost the equivalent to the entire normal export figure for a one and a-half year period.
We overlook the fact that the world's population is also astronomical. There are over 2J billion people and in terms of food reserves we have only 36 pounds of wheat per person. In the United States, where flour consumption is moderate, 190 pounds of wheat a year per person is consumed.
For much of the world population wheat is unobtainable but the annual consumption is in the neighbourhood of 6 billion bushels. A 11 billion bushel surplus is the equivalent to a three-months supply for this wheat-eating section.
Awkward as carryovers may be to world trade, a 90-day reserve supply of such an important food commodity does not seem unreasonable.
I say, Mr. Speaker, few livestock men would care to operate on a narrower basis as far as basic food reserves are concerned. The article goes on to say:
The human race should be able to design an economy that would permit it to carry some assurance against emergency food depletion without causing a marketing breakdown and penalizing the producer.
I mentioned a short while ago that 18 per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in the basic industry of agriculture and they receive less than 7 per cent of the national income. There are many reasons for this. Perhaps one of the reasons for the present condition in which farmers find themselves is that the farmers of Canada are perhaps the only major wheat exporting people in the world who are operating in a purely unprotected market as far as the selling of their products is concerned. The farmers of Canada are finding themselves entwined in a terrific cost-price squeeze. That is perhaps true to some extent of farmers throughout the whole world.
Here I have a short article which gives the over-all position of the farmers throughout some of the major countries of the world. I find that in the period from January 1, 1953 to the end of the first three months of

The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith 1956 the over-all position of the farmers in these countries followed a pattern. In Australia the over-all position of farmers declined 15 per cent; in Canada in that period the position of farmers declined 19 per cent; in Finland the over-all position was up 23 per cent; in West Germany, up 11 per cent; Japan, up 4 per cent; in the Netherlands down 5 per cent; and in the United States down 16 per cent.
I wish to point out that as far as the farmers in Canada are concerned their position declined 19 per cent, more than in any other country shown in this set of figures. This is a sad picture, but it is true. I have never heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) get up on the floor of this house and give a convincing argument against the statement that agriculture in Canada is in a deplorable condition. I am looking forward with interest to his doing so at some time during the present session. I would like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) why he has permitted our basic industry to dip down to such low economic levels. This situation, if allowed to continue, will eventually lead to the complete collapse of our food producing industry. I know that in our own area local government bodies along with businessmen and others who are associated with the farmers are finding it increasingly difficult to carry on as a result of this ever-decreasing income.
In my own municipality of Vermilion river arrears of taxes have risen to the startling figure of $609,715. This means that 36 per cent of all the parcels of land in that municipal district are in arrears of taxes. In the municipal district of Wainwright, which is south of my municipality, a similar condition exists. Arrears of taxes in 1955 had accumulated in that municipality to $267,077 with 108 parcels of land under tax recovery.

speechtext:
Forget . about that. You do not know about that or you would not speak that way. The reason for the great increase in tax arrears in these two municipal districts must be obvious to all, even to my hon. friend the member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). It simply means that the farmers of these districts do not have the cash with which to pay their taxes. I know of many farmers who for the first time since the depression years have had to forgo the payment of their annual taxes.
I now wish to spend a few moments on a matter which is of concern in this house. It is the unfairness of the present existing floor prices on hogs. When one considers that 90 per cent of the hogs exported from Alberta in 1955 found their way to markets
[Mr. Smith (Battle River-Camrose) .1

in British Columbia and that it costs only $1 per hundredweight to ship a hog from Edmonton to Vancouver, how can the Minister of Agriculture justify the wide spread in the floor prices on hogs that exists between the Edmonton and the eastern markets of Toronto and Montreal? The floor price for Edmonton is $18.50 per hundredweight and $23 per hundredweight on the Toronto-Montreal market. Surely if there is any justice at all in the differential of floor prices for hogs across Canada or any justice at all for this spread the minister would establish a floor of $22 per hundredweight on the Edmonton market.
The farmers of Alberta raise good hogs. They would raise more if they were assured of a fair return for their labours. The drastic reduction in the number of hogs raised in Alberta last year was a direct consequence of the unstable markets that existed the previous year. At one time Great Britain was a large importer of Canadian pork products, but for reasons best known to the present administration the market has presently disappeared.
I wish to go back to the year 1935 when this present administration took over. That year we exported to Great Britain over one million hogs. In 1940, just at the beginning of the war, we were exporting to Great Britain over 2,800,000 hogs. I am prepared to admit that during the war period there was some increase in the demand for Canadian hogs. At the end of 1945 we exported to Great Britain 3,600,000 hogs. By 1950, five years after the close of the war, the British market had slipped from a high of 3,600,000 to just slightly over 600,000 hogs. Five years later in 1955 we exported to Great Britain 53 hogs. Up until the end of July last year we had not sold Britain one pound of pork products. Surely there is something wrong with the marketing policies of a government which allows such a situation to develop.
I would like to comment briefly on the operation of the agricultural prices support board. The story has been spread across Canada that the operation of this board has cost the taxpayers of Canada a tremendous amount of money. The board was established in 1946. Since 1946 the administration of the agricultural prices support board has cost the people of Canada $89 million. The greatest part of this amount, $70 million, was spent in paying the loss to the farmers of Saskatchewan by reason of the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak in 1952.
The remainder over a ten-year period was allocated in this manner:	$8.5 million for
cost of butter support since 1949; $6.7 million

for apples; and $2 million for potatoes. The other support items are relatively small, not including the foot-and-mouth crisis. In the ten-year period price supports have cost the treasury of Canada less than $2 million per year or about 15 cents per person in Canada per year. That certainly is not an extravagant amount to guarantee to the farmers of Canada support prices.
I turn now to the figures of the bureau of statistics, using as a base the period 1943 to 1945. The estimated parity price on butter in 1956 is 71.6 cents per pound. The average marketing price of first grade butter during the past year was 58.6 cents. As far as hogs are concerned, using the same period, the average market price for B-l hogs across Canada was $25.98, parity $28.87 per cwt. Grade "A" (large) eggs, per dozen in Montreal parity 71.4 cents; the average market price only 58 cents.
I think, Mr. Speaker, it is high time the Minister of Agriculture gave serious consideration to bringing the Agricultural Prices Support Act in line with the parity established for the base period 1943-1945.
At the commencement of this address I suggested that I would request the government to give very serious consideration to certain proposals which I feel would help relieve the crushing burden now borne by Canadian agriculture. I would like to see the present government take immediate action with regard to certain proposals:
1.	A system of cash advances on farm-stored grain, payment of these advances to be administered by some agency other than the Canadian wheat board, and the cost of administration to be borne by the government.
2.	Immediate action to be taken toward the extension of permanent government-owned storage facilities and the renewal of the policy of encouraging the use of temporary off-site storage facilities to enable farmers to deliver their grain.
3.	Introduction of an aggressive and realistic foreign sales policy as far as our agricultural products are concerned.
4.	Opening of a thorough investigation into the merits of the two-price system of marketing our agricultural products with a view to establishing a parity price for all agricultural products.
5.	The marketing of flax and rye to be handled by the Canadian wheat board.
6.	Equalization of the floor prices paid on hogs all across Canada and a raising of these prices to bring them in line with estimated parity using the period 1943-1945 as the base period.
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
7.	Amendments to be introduced to the Farm Loan Act to make this act of some use to young men wishing to enter the agriculture industry.
8.	The enactment of an all-risk insurance plan which will assure the farmers of Canada a just income in case of crop failure or some other disaster.
9.	The acceptance of sterling and the currency of other lands to stimulate trade with those countries, and
10.	The immediate appointment of a transport controller with power to see that there is an equitable distribution of box cars in the west at all times.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the remarks of my colleague for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) and other members of this group in support of their plea for further assistance to the senior citizens of this country, and to make one observation concerning the C.P.R. strike.
This strike meant a nine-day delay with regard to the movement of grain along the C.P.R. lines. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) to use whatever influence they may have toward seeing that grain movement along the C.P.R. system be accelerated as much as possible so that farmers delivering grain at C.P.R. points will not have to suffer any more than necessary as a consequence of this strike.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand it is not customary for the mover or seconder of the address to speak again during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I am informed, however, that as a vote on the first subamendment has been taken, and as a second subamendment has been moved and is presently before us for consideration, it is in order for me to speak again.
Two major problems directly affecting the province of New Brunswick and, I could say, the Atlantic provinces, have been a topic of important discussion during the present debate. One was the recently published preliminary report of the Gordon commission and the other was the question of power development in New Brunswick.
It is not my intention to review what has been said by opposition members with regard to the Gordon commission's preliminary report on the Atlantic provinces. As expected, the report devoted a special section to the problems and difficulties with which people living in the Atlantic provinces must contend.
520	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
Notwithstanding the fact that our average incomes continue to lag behind the average for the rest of Canada, we cannot deny that in the maritimes per capita net incomes have increased by 94 per cent between 1926 and 1955, as compared with an average increase of 80 per cent for the six other provinces.
We all admit that living standards in the Atlantic provinces are lower than in the rest of Canada, and it is our duty as representatives of that region to make a positive and comprehensive approach to our problems. It is not, Mr. Speaker, by painting gloomy pictures of our situation, by crying havoc or despair and by destructive criticism such as we have heard from opposition members that we will contribute to improving our condition or overcome our difficulties.
A number of newspapers and even some men in public life have passed a quick judgment or have expressed their disappointment with respect to certain recommendations contained in this preliminary report of the Gordon commission. Some have been expert enough to extract single sentences and deduce from these their own conclusions. Some have been insulted, scandalized by the suggestion that the government pay the cost of relocation for people who may wish to move away from the maritimes to other areas, and a few, I am sorry to say, must have expressed their opinion without even reading the report.
Constructive suggestions are being made which, I am sure, will receive serious consideration from this government and, I could also add, from provincial and municipal levels. It is a well-recognized fact that inadequacies do exist in our transportation facilities, and appropriate measures should be taken in order to provide solutions. The Gordon report suggests that the "whole question of an improved but integrated system of transportation in the Atlantic region should be examined carefully and in detail, proper consideration being given to the cost involved in providing any new facilities and to the losses being incurred in the operation of existing services". The commission goes further and suggests that "this should be the subject of a special inquiry which will also include in its terms of reference reexamination of the present effects of the Maritime Freight Rates Act". The report urges that this proposed inquiry be undertaken promptly and, upon its completion, that the measures required to improve the present situation should be taken without delay.
Among other suggestions is that of an expanded program of geological surveys, and


that of a land use classification scheme coupled with the provision of assistance to people who may be willing to move to other areas and re-establish themselves in other industries. Suggestions are also being made with reference to our coal industry, and I wish to quote from page 103 of the report, paragraph 13:
We suggest therefore that the emphasis of the present subsidy arrangements should be modified in order to give priority to the greatest possible use of Nova Scotia coal in this region.
We believe that changes in the present subsidy arrangements should include incentives designed to encourage the use of Nova Scotia coal in the generation of thermal power in the Atlantic region.
The use of coal for thermal power should in the future prove to be the main solution to our maritime problems. It will provide work for our miners and power for our industries. Let us be logical. Let us be realistic in our thinking and in our admission of problems and facts with which we must contend. Can we in reality expect the same living standards to prevail throughout our country from coast to coast? Are the living standards in the states of Maine and Vermont comparable to those of California or some of the most industrialized states of our American neighbours? Are the living standards of the Normandy coast of France comparable to the existing conditions along the Mediterranean shores?
What we require, Mr. Speaker, as I have said earlier, is a positive and comprehensive approach to the problem facing us in the Atlantic provinces. We have heard remarks expressed in the house by some opposition members which, if taken seriously, would lead every one of us to leave at once our maritime regions for other parts of Canada.
Let us face facts. We do have in many areas many sections of our Atantic provinces, certain settlements, certain groups, which should never have been allowed to establish themselves in those remote regions where no government assistance, not even substantial hand-outs, could provide the type of living standards which would bring these groups up to a fair basis with other people in the most favoured regions in the country.
What is the actual situation in New Brunswick? I should like to quote a few paragraphs from the annual New Year's message to his people of the premier of New Brunswick, as taken from the Telegraph-Journal of December 31, 1956.
Premier Hugh John Flemming expressed confidence in his annual New Year's message to the people of New Brunswick that 1957 will be "a year of outstanding achievement" for the province.
Further on there are these words:
I see no reason why I should qualify or subtract from that prediction in any way since, month by

month and week by week, everyone in this province has been conscious of living in a new and vigorous atmosphere of enterprise and well-being. This feeling of ours has been strongly supported by statistics. For instance, the index figure for employment in the province was 111.4 in September, 1955. In September, 1956, the figure had risen to 116.7.
Again he says:
Upon the basis of statistics for the first three quarters of 1956 we are entitled to predict that 1957 will be a year of outstanding achievement.
He goes on further and enumerates some of the industries which have started in New Brunswick. He says:
Private industry has invested many millions of dollars in new plant capacity in our province. One of the largest long lumber mills in our history is about to go into production in the Saint John area. Expansion of pulp and paper capacity has also gone forward. All major manufacturing industries have been very active. Smaller plants and new industries have, perhaps, shown the greatest expansion of all. The frozen foods processing industry, new to our province, will soon have two new units in production.
In this case, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize the fact that if these two new plants will soon be in existence it is due to assistance from the federal treasury. Speaking about Camp Gagetown, he says:
Another favourable factor has been the progress made at Camp Gagetown by the Department of National Defence. This great project will provide further support to the economy of the province during 1957. The addition of a new community at Oromocto is proceeding satisfactorily with the cooperation of defence, provincial and local authorities.
What a contrast, Mr. Speaker, with the gloomy and depressed picture presented to the house only a few days ago by some opposition members. The hon. member for Digby-Anna-polis-Kings has described the Gordon commission report as a doleful report. Let us hear what his premier, Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia, has to say about it. I quote from an article appearing in the Ottawa Journal under date of January 19, 1957. The article is headed, "Stanfield Sees Value for N.S. in Gordon Report." Listen to this:
Premier Stanfield said yesterday it would be "unfortunate" if Nova Scotians "summarily dismissed" Gordon commission recommendations because of suggestions that under certain conditions maritimers be assisted to leave the area.
In a prepared statement outlining his reaction to commission findings, he said Nova Scotians do not consider "shipment of maritimers" westward is the answer, but some of the suggestions "may prove valuable and should be examined on their merits".
"The report calls the attention of the whole of Canada to our problems", he said. "Living standards are lower here than they are in the rest of Canada. Some Nova Scotians think this statement shows us in a poor light, but I think it is the simple truth. Most of us have been saying it for a long time."
He said the commission is to be commended for "seeking answers to our problems".
Statements have been made in the house with regard to power developments in New 82715-34
The Address-Mr. Robichaud Brunswick. I feel that the people of New Brunswick and the people of Canada as a whole are entitled to have placed before them all the facts regarding federal and provincial exchange of views in connection with this power development so essential to New Brunswick's economy.
On September 28, 1950, the governments of Canada and the United States made a joint reference to the international joint commission under the boundary waters treaty of 1909. The purpose of the reference was (a) to determine whether the waters of the Saint John could be more beneficially conserved and regulated; (b) to recommend projects to this end; and (c) to indicate how various interests may be affected and what should be done.
Under date of April 6, 1953 the engineering board made an interim report and the commission itself transmitted this report to the governments on January 27, 1954, and the report was made public on October 28 of the same year. The board's report indicates that the early steps are required to increase the generating facilities in New Brunswick and Maine. It suggested a solution valid to 1961, namely, interconnection of existing power systems in the area, development of Beech-wood and provision of about 600,000 acre-feet of storage in the Saint John river basin above Grand Falls.
As agreed between the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the premier of New Brunswick, on December 14 and 15, 1954, senior federal officials, in conjunction with the New Brunswick commissioners and their advisers, made an on the spot investigation of the proposed hydro developments on the Saint John river. Almost a year later, in October, 1955, I will admit that the premier of New Brunswick sought to ascertain whether federal financial assistance could be made available to New Brunswick for a ten year program of power development.
On January 26, 1956, as reported at page 558 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Northern Affairs and Natural Resources (Mr. Lesage) the following question:
Has the government given consideration to the possibility of co-operating in the over-all power development of the Saint John river system in New Brunswick?
The minister, in answering my question, advised the house that ever since the early plans for further development of power on the upper Saint John river began about ten years ago the federal government had been in close touch with the situation. In concluding his remarks the minister stated that in letters to him and the Prime Minister under date of October 20, 1955, the premier of New Brunswick said, and I quote again from page

The Address-Mr. Robichaud 558 of Hansard, that "New Brunswick would like to submit a suitable memorandum in connection with the matter mentioned at an early date."
On November 1, 1955, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources replied that "such a supplementary memorandum from you covering the specific matters you have in mind would be of great assistance to me." We all know, and this has been made public, that on January 30, 1956, Premier Flemming's proposals were received in Ottawa. They were alternative proposals suggesting that (a) the federal government advance funds for the hydro developments of the Saint John at the prevailing rate of interest of long term government of Canada bonds, the amount required being $89 million in 11 years plus $30 million to develop the Canadian share of the river, or that the federal government advance on the same terms $211 million for hydro and thermal developments in New Brunswick. Following receipt of this proposal the federal government asked the government of New Brunswick for certain data with regard to certain difficulties in ascertaining whether 600,000 acre feet of essential storage can be made available for the further development of Beechwood. It has been made very clear that this storage is essential for the development amounting to $119 million on the Saint John river as suggested in Premier Flemming's first proposal.
Most of us have listened to charge after charge against this government by members of the opposition to the effect that Ottawa has refused to endorse New Brunswick's note for Beechwood, that Ottawa has turned us down flat and a number of similar accusations to that effect.
These two alternative proposals, Mr. Speaker, make it clear that Premier Flemming is not asking the federal government to endorse New Brunswick's note for the construction of Beechwood. The premier of New Brunswick wants more than an endorsement for Beechwood, but he is asking the federal government for financial assistance for the total capital requirements of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission amounting to $211 million.
Following receipt of these proposals, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, knowing that no agreements or arrangements had been made for storage with the province of Quebec and the state of Maine, and realizing that the developments suggested were not feasible without the assurance of a provision for 600,000 acre feet of water storage, wrote to Premier Flemming pointing out whether such storage

could be provided on the Tobique river for further development of Beechwood as suggested in his proposal.
On January 17, last week, as reported at page 338 of Hansard the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, in a question to the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees), clarified the situation by saying this:
Is the hon. member aware that we are still waiting for the data on the possible storage on the Tobique river that we were promised by the government of New Brunswick some months ago in order to be in a position to make a decision on the request of that government?
This, Mr. Speaker, is the situation. These are the facts which should be made known to the people of New Brunswick and to the people of Canada. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), as reported at page 296 of Hansard of January 16, said this:
I do most positively deny that there has ever been put forward the kind of scheme that could be implemented along the lines I have mentioned. There have been general suggestions, that they should get aid, and with those general suggestions we agree, but there has never been put forward any specific proposition that could be recommended to parliament as one that would really stimulate the economy of the Atlantic region in a fashion that would be beneficial to the whole economy of Canada.
As stated in Premier Flemming's New Year's message, there has been notable and continuous progress in the mining industry of the province during the past year. I have more confidence in the present premier of New Brunswick than have most of New Brunswick's opposition members, if we are to judge them by their statements regarding the miserable and depressed condition of our population. As long as New Brunswick's premier recognizes that another factor most favourable to our provincial economy has been the progress made at Camp Gagetown by the Department of National Defence, and as long as our premier admits with all frankness that this great project will provide further support to the economy of the province during 1957, unlike the opposition members I have enough confidence in the sincerity of our premier to believe that he will assist the growth of mining in New Brunswick to secure for our people a maximum of benefit.
I have enough confidence and faith in the future of New Brunswick to believe that the lack of electrical power will not be detrimental to our advancement and to the proper development of our natural resources. Federal authorities in co-operation with the provincial government will see to it that everything possible is done to derive the full benefits from the resources placed at our disposal by Divine Providence. But the federal government must have the information they have requested before they can

give further consideration to the proposals from the province of New Brunswick.
I have now reached the third point of my remarks, Mr. Speaker. During the third session of this parliament I chose to ignore the vicious and false accusations made against me in this house and on the radio by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne). On January 14 the same hon. member, in a speech again noted for substituting abuse for argument and exaggeration for emphasis, saw fit to carry on with new accusations in language not worthy of a member of this parliament. Again I had decided to ignore those attacks and charges. The hon. member may accuse me of being a baby-sitter and an untrue representative of my people but, Mr. Speaker, I want him to know that I am not ashamed of having to baby-sit for my family of nine children. My sincere hope is that I can bring them up to be good citizens of Canada and that they at all times will be polite to their neighbours and never use the type of language and tactics so familiar to the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska.
As a representative of my people, I am not ashamed of my actions in this house and at home. My electors know that I have at heart the welfare and well-being of all my constituents. The charges made by the hon. member reflect not only on individual members but on all members of this house, irrespective of their party. I want to quote from an article entitled "Report from Parliament Hill-J. C. Van Horne, Member Parliament" which appeared in the Camp-bellton Graphic of January 17, 1957. I shall read part of it:
To begin with, I am vexed and put out to see what is going on in Ottawa this week. Here we are with thousands of people, not only in my riding but all over the country, out of work, and here we are with a crippling transportation strike on our hands, and what does the government do: it puts on cocktail parties and receptions. When will this government realize that the people did not put it in office to have fun and parties, but to render good government to the people. With our problems mounting day by day, with suffering and hardship and want the lot of far too many of our people, our government knocks off work-
Listen to this.
-to have fun. What a set-up! Apart from the Governor General's reception Tuesday night I have refused all other invitations in protest against a government which cares too little for the people and too much for frivolity.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, it will now be in order for me to direct the attention of the house to the speech from the throne which is the subject of the debate before us. I notice that this year special emphasis was placed on the subject of external affairs in the speech from the throne. Half of the subject matter of that speech is devoted to Canadian foreign relations. To underline the importance of the subject the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Cardin) have all participated in the debate and have dealt with matters concerning the department. No other cabinet ministers have taken part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is obvious therefore, that the government is paying particular attention to the subject of external affairs this year because of the critical world situation or because of the closeness of an election and the


great dissatisfaction in Canada with the government's action at the time of the Suez crisis.
I think the latter is the correct explanation for this extraordinary state of affairs. I note also that the speech from the throne and the addresses of the two ministers whom I have mentioned have placed special emphasis on the commonwealth of nations. The speech from the throne uses this sentence, and I quote:
My ministers remain convinced of the need to maintain the basic unity of the commonwealth . . .
This is indeed an unusual sentence. No such reference to the commonwealth appears in any speech from the throne from 1949 to the present time. Here and there in the preceding sessions casual reference was made to the commonwealth in those years in which commonwealth conferences were being held but this is the first occasion since 1949 on which the commonwealth has received special attention in the speech from the throne. Hon. members will note the phraseology.
My ministers remain convinced of the need to maintain the basic unity of the commonwealth . . .
The sentence should read as follows: My ministers, and particularly the minister of external affairs, have suddenly discovered the British commonwealth of nations. Heretofore they have been only half conscious of its existence and have made little or no effort to maintain the basic unity of the commonwealth or even mention the subject. Now, in this year of 1957, the Secretary of State for External Affairs devoted a great portion of his speech on January 14 to the commonwealth. He sang its praises; he acknowledged its importance in the world. He considered that it is the first of four factors that influence Canada's foreign policy. He emphasized the necessity of strengthening the commonwealth. Of course, this gave him an opportunity of referring to the alleged break in the commonwealth that he keeps telling us almost occurred at the time of the Suez crisis. This has been one of the major propaganda efforts of the minister. He has placed himself in the position of the saviour of the commonwealth and has implied that, as a result of Canada's action at the United Nations in November under his direction, the Asian members of the commonwealth were retained within this great organization.
Although sufficient evidence has been produced from the statements of the Prime Ministers of Ceylon and India that they did not entertain any idea of withdrawing from the commonwealth, nevertheless the minister and some of his followers on the government side persist in proclaiming him as the man

who saved the commonwealth. I was interested in noting that the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the course of his speech, in which he also emphasized the value of the commonwealth, failed to pay any tribute to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This was an unfortunate oversight because the Secretary of State for External Affairs in his speech expressed his gratitude to the Minister of National Health and Welfare for his activities in strengthening the commonwealth among the Asian members, during the course of his tour of the Far East. I judge from this that the Minister of National Health and Welfare found no evidence of the alleged disruption of the commonwealth which has so possessed the mind of the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
I note that the Minister of National Health and Welfare, in his discussions with our friends in the Far East, told them something about the history of Canada and its relations with the United States, and fell into the same error that the Minister of National Defence did last year, an inaccuracy with regard to our history. The Minister of National Health and Welfare told the people whom he met in the Far East that with respect to the United States-and these are his words-we have "side by side over 140 years lived in peace". Well, I think he is overlooking the fact that during the period from the war of 1812-14 to 1870 relations between Canada and the United States and between Great Britain and the United States were often very strained; that there was considerable difficulty in maintaining the peace; that armed forays were made into Canada by Fenian raiders; that the militia was called out on several occasions to resist them and that the last raid was made in 1870. During the course of those earlier years strenuous efforts were made by the Canadian government to retain in Canada formations of the British army to give us protection. For the benefit of the Minister of National Health and Welfare I shall read to him a small portion of a letter addressed by the Prime Minister of Canada in 1870 to the appropriate cabinet minister in England. Sir John A. Macdonald wrote as follows:
The withdrawal of the troops from Canada is, I think with you, a most unwise and shortsighted proceeding. At this moment we are in daily expectation of a formidable Fenian invasion, unrepressed by the United States government, and connived at by their subordinate officials.
Therefore let us put the date for the peaceful relations between our country and our great neighbour to the south at 1870, which is not 140 years.
In his remarks the Secretary of State for External Affairs stated that it was necessary,
The Address-Mr. Churchill because of recent events, to make a reassessment of the principles which have underlined our policy and the factors that influence them. He then went on to list the four principal factors of Canadian foreign policy and he placed them in this order: the commonwealth, the United Nations, NATO and the United States of America. He placed his greatest emphasis upon the United Nations and, strangely enough, I thought that his discussion of the United Nations was really the swan song of that organization. He mentioned the gap between responsible and irresponsible membership, the impossibility of compulsory enforcement of United Nations proposals, the growing tendency to force through the assembly impractical and unreasonable resolutions merely by voting power and the development of the group or bloc veto in the assembly which may result, as he said, in that body becoming as ineffective as the security council; and, Anally, that the United Nations provides no substitute for the national policies of its members.
This leads me to wonder whether, with these doubts in his mind, the Secretary of State for External Affairs is wise in attempting to create the impression that Canada's foreign policy depends to such a great extent on the United Nations. If that body is no more effective than the minister has pointed out, it is indeed a slender reed on which Canada is leaning in the difficult task of attempting to provide national security and a stable and enduring peace throughout the world.
I think the time has come when we should examine the value of the United Nations as it is constituted at the present time. I think it is the height of folly to place so much dependence on an organization which in the last 10 years has failed to keep the peace, which is its main purpose, and which recently has been shown to be unable to enforce its will as expressed by resolutions of the assembly.
I think it is just nonsense to suggest that the cease-Are which was procured at the Suez canal was the result of resolutions passed by the United Nations. I think that that cease-Are and the withdrawal of the British and French forces were brought about chieAy by the pressure exerted upon Britain and France by the United States.
The United Nations has recently passed a resolution requiring the state of Israel to withdraw its armed forces from the areas formerly held by Egypt, the Gaza strip and the gulf of Aqaba. If the state of Israel does withdraw her forces from those areas it will be because of the economic sanctions applied to Israel by the United States. I draw the

The Address-Mr. Churchill attention of the house to an article appearing in the New York Times of January 20, which reads in part as follows:
Israel was expecting from $25 million to $30 million in grants in aid from the United States this year. She was also planning a $75 million loan from the export-import bank. After the Sinai campaign grants in aid were stopped and there is no word yet that they will be resumed. There is also no commitment on the loan.
I just wonder whether that would have a greater effect on the state of Israel than a resolution passed by the United Nations.
We have recently heard a great deal about the effectiveness of the United Nations in marshalling public opinion. The parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke in the house on January 15 and expressed, I judge, the point of view of the department and of the minister. He said that he was impressed by the unprecedented power and strength of world opinion which was so forcibly expressed at the United Nations not so long ago. He then went on to say, as recorded at page 229 of Hansard:
World opinion has become more than ever before an extremely important factor in the relationship of states, to which no state, no matter how powerful, can afford now to be indifferent.
If world opinion is as powerful a force as this, why was it so ineffective with regard to the disaster that befell the people in Hungary? What effect did world opinion have on Russia during that terrible crisis? The answer is absolutely none at all. If world opinion is such a powerful force, why has it been necessary during the last few years to establish such military alliances as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the Baghdad pact? If it is so powerful, why do we have to spend half of our annual budget for military defence? Why does the United States have to maintain the largest strategic bombing force in the world, with air bases on every continent? Why must we have a stockpile of atom and hydrogen bombs? Why must we spend millions in providing great radar lines in northern Canada? If world opinion is such a powerful force to maintain peace, why is it necessary periodically for the United States to enunciate such policies as containment and massive retaliation? Why is it necessary for the proclamation of the Eisenhower doctrine with regard to the Middle East? If world opinion, as expressed through the United Nations, is such a powerful force, as so many people are telling us, why are all these defensive preparations necessary, why not just another resolution of the United Nations? The answer, of course, is that the belief in the power of world opinion is merely a delusion. The United Nations, as constituted at the present time, can exert only moral suasion. Each nation
IMr. Churchill.]
is a sovereign body. No nation is bound by international law except on its own consent. There is no effective sanction, either military or economic, at the disposal of the United Nations to apply to members who fail to abide by decisions of that organization. Now being tried is an experiment in the use of a method more effective than a resolution made by the United Nations. This is being done by means of the emergency force which is operating on the boundary between Egypt and Israel.
A United Nations police force has been the subject of discussion in many circles for the last ten years. Of course when the minister for external affairs proposed such a force at the United Nations assembly in November it was hailed as a stroke of inventive genius. The Canadian propaganda machine which functions at the United Nations made the most of this opportunity by impressing upon Canadians by means of television, radio and newspaper articles that the Secretary of State for External Affairs was a statesman unparalleled in the history of the world. Disillusionment followed very closely after this momentous discovery, when it became evident that Colonel Nasser had the final word as to the nature of the force, its disposition and the length of its stay on Egyptian soil. Even now, when opinion is in favour of the United Nations police force occupying the Gaza strip and other disputed territories on the border of Israel, Egypt objects to this use of the emergency force.
The latest resolution passed by the United Nations and therefore, so we are led to believe, expressing the power of world opinion, simply insists that Israel withdraw entirely from the disputed area and that a return be made to the status quo. No permanent solution between Israel and her neighbours is in sight. Although this represents a very unpropitious beginning for a United Nations military force, the minister of external affairs is now advocating the provision by members of the United Nations of forces which would be available when the necessity arose to institute international police action. This is what he said on page 177 of Hansard of January 14:
The kind of force we have in mind would be designed to meet situations calling for action, intermediate if you like, between the passing of resolutions and the fighting of a war, and which might incidentally have the effect of reducing the risks of the latter. It would not, however, as I see it, be expected to operate in an area where fighting was actually in progress; it would be preventive and restoratory rather than punitive or belligerent.
The minister is fond of adjectives, uses them skilfully and bemuses us by his use of them. I find it difficult to visualize forces

of this nature being used in the intermediate period between the passing of resolutions by the United Nations and the actual outbreak of war. If the United Nations police force, which is now in the mind of the minister, is no better equipped for offensive or defensive action than the present force now serving in the Middle East, I would think that any member of the United Nations which committed troops abroad under such circumstances would simply be giving hostages to fortune. Without effective support from air, armour and artillery, an infantry police force armed only with rifles, machine guns and mortars is not much more than an enlarged observer corps.
I would like to ask the minister in what area of the world he would see such an international police force stationed. If this is an effective way of dealing with threats to western democracy from Russia would he suggest that a United Nations police force be stationed in Germany, and that the United States and British divisions be recalled, along with the Canadian forces? If we believe all the propaganda to which we have been subjected during the last few months the NATO alliance is obviously unnecessary, and we should place our reliance upon the great power of public opinion expressed by resolutions supported by a majority vote in the United Nations assembly and assisted by a lightly armed infantry force on the borders between hostile states.
I suggest that to base Canada's foreign policy upon the United Nations as our main shield and our main defence against war is nothing short of folly. Until the United Nations has become a much more powerful body than it is at the present time; until the nations of the world are prepared to submit to the rule of law, and until the United Nations is able effectively to enforce its decisions, we are making a great mistake in placing too much reliance on this organization for the preservation of peace.
I submit that the minister must reappraise Canada's foreign policies and rearrange in his thinking the four factors on which he states our policy is based. I am of the opinion that the four factors should be arranged in this order:	first, the commonwealth;
second, NATO; third, the United States of America; and fourth, the United Nations. This, of course, means relying upon military alliances, the age-old method of protection for states which in themselves are not powerful enough to resist any foreign threat. Military alliances have not brought about lasting peace, but have served from time to time to postpone war and on the outbreak of conflict to provide collective security for the members of the alliance.
The Address-Mr. Churchill
There is no immediate prospect of establishing permanent peace in the world. This will only be achieved when some sort of world government is established. No possibility of world government exists at the present time because of the lack of uniformity among the systems of government in the various nations of the world. Dictatorships, oligarchies and democracies can find no common basis for agreement. That leaves us with no alternative except the maintenance of military alliances among the democracies, with the hope perhaps of establishing closer political ties among those nations whose philosophies of life and whose systems of government are similar.
Therefore it is obvious that for the security of Canada-and that is the main function of the Department of External Affairs-our greatest reliance should be placed upon our membership in the British commonwealth, our association with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and our close ties with our powerful neighbour to the south. Every effort should be made by Canada to strengthen the commonwealth and to strengthen the bond between the commonwealth and the United States.
Had this conception of Canada's foreign policy been uppermost in the mind of the minister of external affairs last November I doubt very much if he would have abstained from voting at the United Nations assembly. Abstaining from a vote is an important action in the United Nations assembly. One of the senior civil servants in the Department of External Affairs a few years ago explained the meaning of abstention in the following words'.
To abstain is not a neutral act with no policy implications, not a simple statement of lack of knowledge; it is a definite political act with definable political connotations.
The minister's abstention on the occasion of the vote in November was a definite political act which made a choice between making common cause with the commonwealth and becoming a satellite of the United States. I would direct your attention to a very interesting book entitled "Canada in World Affairs" by B. S. Keirstead, which examines Canada's external relations during the period 1951-53. He deals with the subject which I am now discussing, and on page 44 points out that with regard to Canadian interests abroad the first thing in which we are interested is stable and enduring peace with, as a corollary, security against attack, provision for security directed toward a strong bargaining position for the negotiation of a settlement.
Later, on pages 239 and 240, he deals with the subject of the commonwealth, and is not altogether sympathetic with the policies of

The Address-Mr. Churchill the Department of External Affairs which were pursued in those years and which, as far as I can gather, are being followed at the present time. There is a short quotation here which I think may be of interest. The writer says:
The countries of the commonwealth have a unique organization. With different languages, religions, and national cultures, they share a common political tradition, a common set of moral and political values, and a common habit of mind in the face of political problems. This common habit of mind is one of moderation, of compromise, of negotiation, of give and take. While no common foreign policy is possible, if one means by that an agreed course of action on every issue, anything that might strengthen the presentation of the commonwealth habit of thought would surely be a contribution to world peace. If this is what is meant by closer commonwealth collaboration in foreign policy, and it is all that it is possible to mean, then it does make sense to ask if the extreme official caution in Canada and the sensitivity to anything that might even appear to make Canadian policy depend on London has been justified. After all, if the choice is between making common cause with London occasionally (and New Delhi, Canberra, Colombo, and others) and becoming a satellite of the United States, anyone who values, or even has valued, Canadian independence ought not to have difficulty in seeing where the danger lies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have suggested the order of the factors upon which I think Canada should place its reliance, dealing with the factors originally enunciated by the minister for external affairs, I should think now that he has seen the light, we would be in agreement concerning the commonwealth. After all, why should there ever have been any separation from the commonwealth on the part of Canada? Our roots have never been cut from the homelands from which the two great races of this country have sprung, and in those difficult periods of the twentieth century when vital decisions had to be made, in 1914 and 1939, there was no serious difference of opinion among the Canadian people as to what should be their decisions. We were not disturbed, or waiting to see what Washington would say with regard to what action we should take. Nor was it a question simply of saying "Ready, aye ready" as the minister tries to imply. It was because of our common background of thought and belief that we faced the problems that confronted the world in those two wars in the way we did, and were ready to defend the cause of freedom and democracy.
The second factor, Mr. Speaker, is our relation with NATO. It is a military alliance, but what is the alternative to a military alliance in so far as we are able to discover at this stage of world development? It is a strong military alliance in which we place our greatest hope. If we did not have the benefit of that alliance we would be in grave danger. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the

minister of external affairs should place much more emphasis in this house on the subject of NATO than he does.
The propaganda machinery which is consistently telling us about the minister's speeches at the United Nations does not seem to operate at all with regard to NATO conferences, with the result that NATO is a relatively unknown quantity among Canadians. This is true to such an extent that in the last two years, when representatives of this House of Commons and of the other house have gone to a conference attended by representatives from all the other members of the NATO alliance, certain people have poked fun at the expedition and called it a junket and a joyride at the expense of the people of Canada.
On the contrary, that type of consultation and conference is, I think, essential. If the NATO alliance is to be maintained there must be understanding among the members of NATO and exchanges of opinion from time to time. I am one of those, Mr. Speaker, who willingly look forward to a broader basis for NATO, and I have spoken in this house with regard to the suggestion that an Atlantic alliance might be established as the next step forward in the development of relations among the nations, an alliance which would comprise those nations bordering on the Atlantic who have similar systems of government, a similar background and the capacity for joining together much more closely than in the past in order to make themselves secure in a very insecure world.
The third factor on which we must place our reliance is of course, Mr. Speaker, the United States of America; not in the position of a blind follower of the United States but as a partner in our own right, with the power to influence United States opinion. We have to be extremely careful at the present time about our relationship with the United States. We have been reading in the papers recently about the new policy announced there, and it is interesting to note that Mr. Dulles has been telling us what might happen in the event of trouble. The Globe and Mail of Saturday, January 19, reports what Mr. Dulles said before a Senate committee, and I quote his words:
If we got into war we'd expect to get help from 42 nations with whom we have collective security agreements.
Then he went on to say with regard to consultation:
The United States ought not to have its polices fixed by consultations and agreements with other nations.

Well, Mr. Speaker, much was said in November about the lack of consultation. Now we are informed by this great power that consultation is perhaps not necessary. What position is Canada in? We have United States troops living in our country; we have United States air bases on the soil of Canada. Are we immediately committed in the event the United States takes some action? The closest relationship with the United States is naturally essential to our safety; but, Mr. Speaker, it must be a relationship entered into with ourselves as a partner.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that consideration should be given to these factors in the order in which I have presented them, and I think it would be wise for the House of Commons and the minister for external affairs to take a second look at the policy which was placed before us for consideration the other day. Where does the United Nations come in? I place it at the bottom of the list, not because I think it is completely ineffective; that is not so. The United Nations is an essential part of man's struggle toward securing peace and order in the world. It is at present ineffective, as we know, as an instrument for ensuring and maintaining peace but it has, nevertheless, to be maintained as an organization; indeed, it has to be strengthened in the light of recent events. The weakness of that body should surely be known to all, and it is because we recognize that weakness, I maintain, that we should not place our full reliance upon the United Nations alone.
We must regard these things in the proper order, the commonwealth, NATO, the United States of America, and after that we should play our full part in the United Nations in order to make it an effective force for the peace we would like to see in the world. But to establish it as the basis of our foreign policy would be, I think, to delude our people. We cannot expect to have peace in the world simply by way of resolutions passed at the United Nations. In this difficult twentieth century, in this period in which we are living in fear of a very destructive war, we must place our reliance upon our known friends, upon our known means of protecting ourselves. It is only as we do that and emphasize these aspects first that we can safely go on to deal with the United Nations and endeavour through that body to reach the solution that everybody in the world hopes for, with the exception perhaps of some of the communist countries.
I do not think there is any doubt in anybody's mind that the average man in the world wants peace. He does not want to be shot at or killed. He is not interested in the destruction of war. He wants peace. But how
The Address-Mr. Churchill is it to be obtained? Let us not delude ourselves into thinking that it can be obtained by an organization whose only effective function at the present time is to determine by a majority vote what resolutions shall be passed at that assembly. The marshalling of public opinion that we hear so much about these days has not been an effective factor in maintaining peace. It is all to the good. We want public opinion marshalled. We want these things brought out into the open. Nations that are oppressed or suffering should be heard.
It is a good thing that in the United Nations all nations of the world there assembled can talk about the disaster that befell the Hungarian people. That shows to them and to all of us everywhere the evil in the world that is represented by communist Russia. But to base our foreign policy on the United Nations as our mainstay is, I think, wholly wrong. We must revise our thinking and start with these other factors in our minds. We must strengthen the commonwealth, strengthen NATO, strengthen the tie with the United States of America, and then from that point use our influence in the United Nations.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join hon. members of the house in congratulating the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do not intend to be very long, because my conviction is that Liberal legislation is very good.
Such testimony from a Liberal member will not surprise anyone, but if I mention it I do so because of the obvious approval of the official opposition, the Progressive Conservative party. Indeed, I have read carefully the program of the Conservative party at its last convention, and I have found that as a whole it constitutes the best appraisement of Liberal legislation in this country. The biggest difference is that the Progressive Conservative party will need about $7 billion or $8 billion to realize their program, instead of $5 billion which is the present budget. One may hope that by 1965 or before the Liberal party will be able to fulfil such an ideal social program.
As there is nothing very controversial in present politics, I should like to say a few words on a subject that should appeal to all members of the house without regard to party lines. I refer to the project of simultaneous translation of speeches in the House of Commons in both official languages of this country. I am sure of finding a sympathetic reception for such a proposal which will please greatly nearly one-third of the members of the house and as many as 5 million people of French descent in this country. We all know that at the United Nations and in many private organizations simultaneous translation is widely used. On May 22, 1956, the Junior Chamber of Commerce of Canada, embracing almost 25,000 members, presented a brief to the Speaker of this house recommending such a system for the House of Commons.
May I add that on the east side of the Ottawa river 4 million people speak French, and the great majority of them are unable to follow the debates of the house when they come here to visit us. Two years ago, Mr. Speaker, I received in Ottawa 200 farmers and their wives from my constituency, and I was sorry that they were unable to follow the debates from their seats in the galleries. My conviction is that the most important


way to promote national unity is to permit a good understanding of the other language. The United Nations organization would have been impossible without simultaneous translation, and all French Canadians going to New York to attend the United Nations meetings come back with the idea that such a system should be in use in the House of Commons.
We should admit that the present system of acoustics is far from being perfect. It is maintained at great cost but it could be replaced with better results so far as hearing is concerned by one system of individual earphones. These earphones could be utilized for both acoustics and simultaneous translation purposes. Here are a few figures on the cost of the present sound system in the
chamber:
Original cost of installation .... $33,529
Annual rental of equipment	 7,500
Operation and maintenance yearly ..	20,000
The wiring was done by public works personnel, and the cost is. not readily available. In the brief of the Canadian Junior Chamber of Commerce already mentioned I see that the cost of installation of a simultaneous translation system in the House of Commons is estimated at $6,272. This means that the installation and operating cost of such a system would be less than for the one we already have and it would give much better results and satisfaction to members in general as well as to the public.
I have in my hand some information about the cost of earphones for public seats at the United Nations. It is approximately $15 per seat. As there are 626 seats in the galleries of this chamber, the total cost for earphones for all the public seats would be $9,390. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I know this parliament is very sensitive to the prerogatives and rights of parliament. I personally feel that parliament is right in defending those rights, because parliament is the means by which good democracy may function. But I think the first condition for a good parliament is that all speakers be understood in their own language when it is possible. I think it is not very good for a parliament that a third of the members speak for the ceilings, for the walls, or just for the press. I believe it should be the right of everyone to be understood in his own language and to hear and speak in his own language.
We feel here that when we speak French this house is not interested. I do not think I will be disagreeable to my English speaking colleagues when I say this. If the situation were reversed and they were in our position, with a third of this house speaking English and we, two-thirds, speaking only

French, I feel sure that the third you would represent would ask strongly for simultaneous translation.
One day I heard a minister say that the members from the province of Quebec did not seem much interested in the legislation of this country outside the province of Quebec. I admit that there seems to be some truth in that observation. However, I think one of the main reasons is the fact that 75 members are obliged to follow the speeches in another language. As we live in a democracy, under a democratic system in which we believe, and which we want to defend, with a parliament that we want to protect, I believe we should have a system that permits everybody to hear and to speak in his own language and not be obliged to speak just for the walls, for the ceilings or for the press. I think we have a right to have that opportunity. When I say that I assure you that it is not from a nationalistic point of view; it is simply on the basis of a democratic system which we want to preserve and which we cherish.
This year I intend to present a resolution on this matter. If I speak on this question in the debate on the speech from the throne it is simply because I want to direct the minds of hon. members to this question which, for us, is extremely important. I have heard the comments made by French speaking members of this house. If you want to be fair to this important minority, I think something should be done. Actually 25 or 30 years after the invention of this system of sound reproduction and simultaneous translation which was used at the first United Nations meetings, I think it is time something should be done in this house. I was told that the actual system of sound reproduction could be installed at small cost, and could be so organized that it would provide simultaneous translation.
On the day I come back with a resolution on simultaneous translation in this house I hope I shall receive approval and sympathy from all sides of this house. Starting from the principle that varied cultures constitute a national enrichment, I think there is no better place than the House of Commons to demonstrate the value of such a principle.
