speechtext:
In preparing my thoughts for what I was going to say tonight, Mr. Speaker, I was reminded of a little tribute which I have wanted to pay in this house almost since the day I came to Ottawa. I think I should do so now. I wish to remark on the unusual courtesy and kindness of the Ottawa taxi drivers.
As one who has been in most of the cities of Canada and many of those of the United States, and used taxicabs in each one of them, I have found that while they may be a very efficient method of transportation, the drivers do not go out of their way to look after one as an individual. I have been tremendously impressed with the difference here in Ottawa. They meet us at the station; they carry our bags up the stairs at home, and this last is an unusual factor which I do think deserves recognition from those of us who come to this city from outside. Incidentally, I may say it is probably a very profitable operation for the taxi driver, because the tips one gives here in Ottawa are considerably larger

The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton in proportion to those one is tempted to give in any other city of which I know.
The Gordon commission report on the economic prospects of Canada over the next 25 years contains some interesting statistics for all of us who live in the cities of Canada. The commission found:
Canada has been becoming an increasingly urban country and this trend will continue. In 1951, 62 per cent of the population lived in metropolitan areas or in other cities, towns or villages with more than 1,000 people. By 1980 that proportion may rise to 80 per cent. Over the same period the proportion of the population living in metropolitan and urban areas of more than 100,000 people may rise from 36 per cent to 56 per cent.
Translated into actual population figures, the commission estimated that by 1980 the population of Canada's 15 metropolitan areas will be some 12 million people, as compared with 5.2 million at our last census. When we turn to Montreal, with which perhaps I am more familiar than with the other metropolitan areas of Canada, we find that while the Gordon commission has not published a particular estimate for that city, other authoritative figures place our population by 1980 at over 3| million, which is an increase of more than l\ million above the present figure.
Let me turn again to the Gordon report to obtain further background for what I am going to say. It forecasts that there will be a steady decrease in the number of hours we will work each week, so the present average of just over 41 hours will be reduced by 1980 to just over 34 working hours per week. It is probable, too, that we shall have a good deal more money to spend because, to quote the report:
By 1980 the average Canadian, after paying income tax, will have about two-thirds again as much net income for his own use as he had in 1955.
I would say in parenthesis, Mr. Speaker, that the Gordon commission is apparently forecasting a Conservative government, because we certainly have indication that the attitude of the present administration is to do nothing except follow up increased income with increased income taxes.
Encouraging as these estimates may be, they foreshadow the further growth of a problem which is already a major one in most of our cities in Canada, and nowhere more so than in our city of Montreal. I refer to the problem of traffic. The figures forecast a tremendous increase in the nature and the extent of that problem over the next 25 years. That is because, first, we have an increasing concentration of our population in and around the major urban centres of Canada. Second, we have an absolute growth in the number of people who are living in those areas.

Third, we have an increase in their spare time, which will be reflected in additional travelling and additional movement around the city itself. Fourth and finally, I think we can expect that the increased income which is forecast will be reflected in increased automobile ownership, as people move from no car to one car and as our families become more and more two-car families where now they operate only a single automobile.
Take as one example Montreal, which is Canada's largest city-and by all indications it is destined to remain so

situated on an island contiguous to other islands. It faces across the St. Lawrence river another area promising, upon the completion of the seaway, to be one of the most prosperous urban areas in Canada if not in the world. The free circulation of traffic, its smooth movement without delay not only throughout the city but across the water barrier which surrounds the city, becomes not only a municipal concern, not only a provincial concern, but a problem of national importance in which, I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, the federal government should have a very direct and immediate interest.
While I have used Montreal as an example, Mr. Speaker, I make these observations on traffic not only in respect of our city but in respect of all the other metropolitan areas across this country which are faced with this problem and which are going to have to solve it, if it is to be solved, through the expenditure of immense amounts of money.
Let me turn to the area which I am using as an example. We find ourselves in Montreal in the midst of a mighty and dynamic metropolitan region which stretches southward to the United States border, westward to the Ontario border, northward in to the Lauren-tians and eastward to the Richelieu river and beyond. Like all the other major cities of Canada, all this surrounding area which is contiguous to the city itself is a part of its region. The city lives, breathes and has its being only as it engages in commerce and interchange of people and business with the metropolitan region surrounding it. As this great heartland of ours grows and flourishes -and I think that future is destined for it- there is going to be an ever greater and more difficult traffic problem throughout the entire area. The co-ordination of this traffic will be the first concern, obviously, of any municipal government or any metropolitan regional government which is established. Once established it will, with the financial help of the provincial government, probably be competent to deal with the arterial roads which run through it and which bind its economic

activities to the rest of the region. But even with a full measure of provincial help no local authority can cope with the many water crossings which this network of arterial roads would require. What demands are likely to be made in the future, and what are the requirements at the present time?
Engineering experts have calculated that it will take a tunnel perhaps seven or eight miles in length to take trains as well as automobiles under the St. Lawrence river, and that this would cost approximately $175 million. I do not propose to quarrel with the cost, though it does seem rather high at this point. I do not even propose to quarrel with the proposed length of the tunnel, though I think we should remember when considering a problem such as this the experience of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the Rockies, where they found that spiral tunnels in which the railroad mounted around and above itself enabled them to bring the road out at a point almost immediately above that at which it entered the mountain. I think that is something which might well be considered by those who are giving this problem engineering study.
Be that as it may, we have a cost estimate of some $175 million in order to provide a tunnel to allow train traffic to go underneath the St. Lawrence river and thus remove it from continued interference with the seaway. That in turn would enable the Victoria and the C.P.R. bridges to be converted to traffic use alone.	Since the
gradient for autos could be much steeper the ends could be raised, especially the south end, to enable it to clear the seaway and thus eliminate another problem which currently is facing us in that area. We also have the promise of the Minister of Transport to deliver a new bridge to Montreal called the Nuns' island bridge, and I shall deal with this subsequently.
With the situation as presently outlined, and with another proposed bridge to the north upon which it is expected the provincial government will embark in the spring, we would still require two additional bridges to the east and west ends of the island, and these might be constructed with the help of the province. On the basis of present-day automobile ownership and traffic count, with these extra bridges and tunnels we would then be almost competent to handle today's traffic. I think I should underline and mark well that I am referring to today's requirements and not those of the future.
Let us look a little into the future. As I have pointed out before, it is estimated that there will be a population increase of about
The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton 1J million in that area by 1980. It is estimated also that motor car registration will increase by about 20,000 a year. This means that in addition to today's traffic, by 1981 there will be an additional 500,000 cars to contend with. We can add to that the increase in the surrounding areas which will rise as the seaway is completed and as industry moves in with its buildings and plans.
This is a clear indication that unless we build well beyond today's requirements we are going to be facing bridge congestion and the blocking of traffic circulation on an even greater scale than at the present time. In order to deal with future requirements we would need at least four more bridges across the St. Lawrence, elevated to clear the seaway traffic, as well as other bridges to the north connecting with the arterial roads.
The cost of such a program is stupendous. Taking the cost of the seven or eight mile tunnel at $175 million, and $90 million each for four elevated bridges which would total $360 million, we arrive at a grand total of $535 million. Then there would be another $300 million to pay for the bridges to connect with the expressways, which would make a grand total of $835 million or close to $1 billion as Montreal's share in providing what would be necessary to deal with the expanding problem of Canadian traffic.
This figure of $835 million to cover the bridges and their immediate connections is obviously impossible of attainment even by such a great metropolis as the city of Montreal. Viewing provincial finances for as short a period as 20 years, it would appear to be even beyond the capacity of the province. If these problems are to be solved it means that they must be considered a responsibility of the federal government. I think I have outlined previously some of the reasons why traffic should be the concern of the federal government as well as the provinces and the municipalities.
In order to arrive at a basis of comparison as to how the federal government might deal with a situation like this we could perhaps turn to the experience of the United States, where at the last session of congress there was created a federal highway administration charged with the building of some 41,000 miles of roads and crossroads to be free of traffic intersections and devoted only to the fast and efficient movement of traffic in the area. They propose to spend some $50 billion in the next 13 years, or approximately $4 billion a year.
One of the major goals of this program is the elimination of traffic congestion in and around big cities by taking the traffic
S50	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton over, under or around the cities by means of bridges, tunnels and underpasses. On the basis of this $50 billion being spread over some 13 years it is expected the United States government will be contributing some $3.2 billion annually by 1965.
Let us relate that to the Canadian picture. On the basis of the relationship between the gross national product of Canada, which is approximately $28.5 billion, and that of the United States, which is about $409 billion, the proportionate amount for us to spend on highways would be some $223 million a year. On the basis of the relationship between our populations, about 16 million in Canada and 167 million in the United States, the proportionate amount would be some $317.5 million a year. Averaging these two figures, which would perhaps give us the truest comparison, we find that the amount would be approximately $270 million if we were to equal the present program of the United States government in highway construction in proportion to our gross national product and our population.
Now let us take a look at just what this government has actually done, and is doing, in this field. The government has acknowledged its responsibility to provide at least some measure of assistance for highway construction across the country by its contribution under the trans-Canada highway plan. In 1955-56 the contributions under this plan were just over $16 million. In the current year they amount to some $30 million. I noticed in the estimates today that another $30 million is proposed for the coming year. To this we must add the construction expenditures by the government itself in connection with providing links in the trans-Canada highway in its own parks. This comes to about $11 million in the current year.
Thus we arrive at a total expenditure for this highway program on the part of the present federal government of about $41 million, and we can use that as a basis of comparison with the $270 million which would be the logical expenditure by this government if it wished to institute a national program of highway development comparable for our country with that undertaken in the United States, and which they feel they can successfully underwrite.
Obviously not even a major part of that amount would be spent in the Montreal area, but if we take our fair share along with Dogberry and Tumbletown, wherever they may be-I use those names so nobody will accuse me of comparing our city with any other-we would receive approximately $38 million a year were such a program instituted.

dealing, Mr. Speaker, with the federal house, and I have not yet reached the point where I receive any instructions from the premier of my province.

Mr. Speaker, I would just love to see any one of the gentlemen on the treasury bench really get down to this question and deal honestly with the premiers of our Canadian provinces and, more particularly, with the premier of Quebec, respecting their views, taking cognizance of local conditions and making a sincere attempt to co-operate with them. speechtext: There are no strings attached to trans-Canada highway money.

have set this plan forward, Mr. Speaker, as an example of the imaginative thinking which I believe is required by the government at the present time in this field of national development. One could go ahead and use many other illustrations; one could find many other fields in which similar action is necessary, but I think this suggestion which I have put forward parallels the attitude of governments which existed in the past, and which helped us to build this country and bring it forward with great strides in a short period of time. I refer, of course, to the time when we were building railroads and canals and when, with federal government assistance, projects which could never have been envisaged either as private or even as provincial projects came into being.
We have reached a point at which traffic in our major cities is strangling the commerce of those cities in a way we have not known before. The federal government, with its tendency to grasp for itself such a large proportion of the tax dollar, has left neither the municipalities nor the provinces with sufficient revenue to deal unaided with this particular problem and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is high time this government proceeded to do something adequate about the situation.
Let us ask ourselves for a moment what this Liberal government has done or what it is proposing to do. How much money has been contributed, for example, toward the situation in Montreal, which I have outlined,

to help in the construction of arterial roads, tunnels and bridges? It has agreed to compensate us for the impairment of traffic caused by the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway by raising one end of the Mercier bridge and the Jacques Cartier bridge, and installing alternate lift bridges at the end of the Victoria bridge. This so-called generosity on the part of the government is intended to restore us to the position in which we were, and we know what that means; choked bridges, highways blocked for miles, helicopters reporting minute by minute news of the blockage, waste of gasoline and waste of time.
It is true we have been promised an additional bridge at Nuns' island at a cost of some $80 million in view of the additional circulation of traffic which is expected to result from activity alongside the seaway, but this project, again, is related to immediate traffic, and it is going to leave us, when completed, in much the position that we are in now.
I wonder, too, Mr. Speaker, whether there is not some contingency in connection with this promised bridge. Before the federal election in 1949 this Liberal government promised a rail and traffic tunnel under the St. Lawrence which was at that time to have cost $80 million or $90 million; the present figure is $175 million. And this present Liberal government was to have paid two-thirds of the cost of this tunnel. There were big headlines in the Montreal newspapers-I read some of them to the Minister of Transport last year -about this statement, this promise of the government. But once the elections were over it was explained that the building of this tunnel was contingent upon the province of Quebec going ahead with power development in the vicinity of the Victoria bridge. We still have not got the tunnel, and last year when it was drawn to the minister's attention he spoke in such a way that we have not even got the promise any more.
When we turn to the promised Nuns' island bridge I think we are right in being a little disturbed. About a year ago we were left with the impression that the construction of the bridge was imminent. We proceeded to a point where the Minister of Transport issued, under date of August 17, 1955, a statement on the development of facilities for the movement of motor traffic between the island of Montreal and the south shore. In that statement the minister said:
. . . the government has decided that it would be in the general interest if the building of a new bridge, with four traffic lanes, connecting the Montreal north shore with the mainland on the south shore were to be undertaken forthwith. Accordingly, instructions have been given to the national harbours board to retain the services of competent engineers to design a bridge to cross the St. Lawrence river over Nuns' island and to
The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton
take, in co-operation with the provincial government and with the municipal authorities concerned, such further steps as are necessary for the building of this bridge. Legislation for these purposes will be recommended to parliament at its next session.
Let me repeat that last sentence.
Legislation for these purposes will be recommended to parliament at its next session.
I have studied with great care the proceedings of the last session of parliament. I have gone through the index, I have searched in every possible place, and there is no legislation whatsoever relating directly to this proposed bridge. There is no specific indication whatsoever that the government has any intention of proceeding with the construction of the bridge.
I think we should realize that the last major project of this kind, the Jacques Cartier bridge in Montreal, was authorized by legislation in this house because it was a matter of joint municipal, provincial and federal concern, and that therefore it would be expected that legislation would be introduced in the house if the government planned to proceed with this project. The fact that they have not introduced such legislation, as so clearly promised in the words of the minister's own statement on August 17, 1955, seems to me to indicate that this also is a project which is contingent upon some other matter.
Only a day or two ago I asked the Minister of Transport when he planned to begin construction of this bridge, and in effect his answer was that he did not quite know, that they hoped to begin some of the approaches this spring. But he cannot begin the approaches and he cannot proceed, as I understand it, until such time as he has got legislation through the house. I suggest most strongly that even if it is a year late, he now make good the promise contained in his statement that he would take action.
I should like finally to touch for a moment on a project which I think might be considered by the government that would be of some considerable benefit to the national development of Canada. I refer to the taking of a national inventory of our natural resources right across the country from coast to coast and the correlation of this information in one particular department where it can be kept up to date. The members of the Gordon commission in their own way have taken an inventory of our economic resources, but we find that we have throughout the country, as we all know, immense natural resources which have been assessed by the provinces but the information on which has not been brought together at one central point.

The federal government have made a start in that connection with their inventory of forest resources under which, in co-operation with the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis, they are taking a complete inventory of the forest resources of our country, but I think that could be extended. subtopic: IMMIGRATION
IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave, pursuant to standing order 26, to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the gross abuse of natural justice constituted by the methods followed at the hearing of the appeal of Christian George Hanna by an immigration appeal board in Vancouver, British Columbia, and the urgent necessity of suspending action in connection with the deportation of Mr. Hanna until his case has been fully considered and disposed of in accordance with proper and just procedures.
If I may, as to the urgency-

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I think the other day the hon. gentleman objected to anything being said after such a motion had been submitted to the Speaker for his opinion.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: And I recall that on that occasion the Speaker said the matter of urgency might properly be the subject of reference, and there was in fact a reference to that question by the right hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I will first read the motion and see if I need any assistance. If I do, no doubt I will call upon the hon. gentleman. It strikes me on reading over the subject matter of the motion which the hon. member for Kamloops has submitted that, as a ground for the urgency of debate in this matter, he talks about the suspension of an action which is about to be taken with respect to the gentleman mentioned in the motion. Perhaps the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill) could state whether or not there is an action contemplated having to do with the deportation of Mr. Hanna.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all I can state is what I hear on the radio and read in the press: that a gentleman who purports to be the solicitor for this person has applied to the supreme court of British Columbia, from which it would seem to me
that the case is before the courts and, therefore, hardly an appropriate subject for debate in this house.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Perhaps I could say what I was told by the solicitor?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That following the process, which was called a hearing, before the immigration appeal board yesterday morning, the man was ordered to leave and was, according to my information at the time of the telephone call, in the process of being transported back to Port Alberni where the boat is lying in harbour and from which it is due to sail, I believe, tonight. Knowing the practice of the department in the past of disregarding notices of applications for writs of certiorari and their practice of trying to get people out of the country notwithstanding those notices having been served, unless the minister is able to state positively that this man will not be deported until after the case is heard, I submit there are grounds established by the wording of the motion for urgency of discussion and decision.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman talks about urgency of discussion and decision. The only decision we can arrive at is that we adjourn the house, and the debate is over. That is the only decision we can arrive at today. The overriding practice, of course, is that while the debate on the address is currently proceeding, motions under standing order 26 are not accepted, and that has been the case, as the hon. gentleman knows, for many years.
There is no doubt that the matter referred to in this motion is one which many members regard with a great deal of sympathy, but as for putting aside the debate on the address today in order to discuss this matter-one which the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has alleged may be before the courts -I hesitate to do so.
One must not forget that there has been moved a subamendment to the amendment on the main motion, and that today and tomorrow, if we go on with the debate on the address, members who have spoken on the main motion or on the amendment may speak again on the subamendment which was moved a few days ago.

Immigration-C. G. Hanna

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
On that particular question, Mr. Speaker, may I say that the purpose of a motion such as this is to enable the house to deal in a substantive manner with the subject matter complained of or brought to its attention. The only way that effective action can be taken in this instance is if we obtain from the minister, as a result of that process and discussion, an assurance that this man will not be sent out of Canada pending full and proper disposition of his case.
There is no way in the course of the speech from the throne debate in which that issue can be brought to a head. It can, I submit, only be brought to a head if you allow me to present this motion so that discussion can be directed towards that specific subject matter and the house can express its opinion and get a positive reaction and assurance from the minister on that basis. There is no way in the throne speech debate to bring about such a result. That is why it is urgent that that debate be adjourned.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Without purporting to give an opinion on the rules, are we not in danger of forgetting that this is the high court of parliament and are there not occasions when we may take such action as will try to ensure that natural justice will be done and that a department of this government, which after all is subject to this house, shall not be allowed to disregard the procedures of the law of the land?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there seems to be no other means whereby a measure of justice can be secured for this man than through a motion such as has been moved by the hon. member for Kamloops. The situation is simply this. If discussion takes place on the speech from the throne debate there is no means whereby the minister may be required to answer in any way and whereby parliament can act in order to prevent anything in the nature of a tyrannical use of absolute power.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I suggest that whatever the merits of the Hanna case may be there is no other recourse. Unless this motion is allowed, then, whatever the courts may subsequently decide, this man may be spirited away and may be out of the jurisdiction and an injustice will have been done. Indeed, to a great degree this is similar to the Archer Shee case. Parliament must necessarily act in order to assure justice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
In view of the interventions of so many gentlemen on the other side, I think possibly the hon. member for Kamloops will feel that the suggestion he made the other day is not of


universal application. There seems to be one question about which it would be quite important to know what the facts are. It is suggested that the solicitor who has been giving information to the hon. member for Kamloops so that it might be used on the floor of the house has made an application to the supreme court of British Columbia for some kind of writ. I do not know whether or not that is a fact. I did not hear the radio reports this morning because I was still on a railway car. But if that is the case then though this may be the highest court of the land there is a positive rule that this highest court of the land has adopted and that is that matters sub judice before the ordinary courts of the land will not be debated here while they are before those courts.
When this is likened to other cases, it seems to me that the suggestion being made is that the department of immigration might be about to do something which was done by the Department of Justice presided over by Hon. Mr. Doherty in 1911 when Harry K. Thaw happened to be within the confines of this country and Mr. Doherty gave instructions, in spite of the proceedings that were before the court, to have him picked up like a chip and just tossed over the border. Nothing of that kind is contemplated here at this time.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: There is not very much similarity between the Harry Thaw case and the present one.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It has never appealed to this government to follow the effective but extraordinary procedures that were adopted in 1911. Proceedings have been taking place in the manner prescribed by the statute and there is the suggestion-and perhaps the hon. member for Kamloops would be in a position to say whether or not this is so-that the solicitor who has been briefing him about this extraordinary case was applying to the courts of justice in the province of British Columbia where I assume that, if there are rights, they can be asserted and will get consideration from the judicial authority in the hon. gentleman's own province.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I point out that I think we are losing sight of what this resolution really asks. I refer to "the urgent necessity of suspending action in connection with the deportation of Mr. Hanna until his case has been fully considered and disposed of in accordance with proper and just procedures". We have before us no information as to what is happening in the supreme court of British

Columbia. However, we have before us information that this man is likely to be deported.
With regard to the matter of urgency may I say this, Mr. Speaker. The other day, when objection was taken to a motion that I made in this house, you were good enough to say that you would look into the matter because there was some doubt in your mind as to whether the debate on the address which is now proceeding ruled out the possibility of a debate on a matter of great urgency. I submit that this is a matter of urgency. I can understand the legal position of the department but I also understand that the final authority with regard to these cases rests with the minister. Here we are, as has already been said by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), sitting here as it were as the high court of parliament, the last court of appeal. We do not know what is happening in British Columbia. We do not know whether the supreme court has allowed the case to be made before it. We know nothing of these things except the word given us by the hon. member for Kamloops. I think the hon. member for Kamloops has a. right to receive information on matters of any kind brought to him by anybody who approaches him with authentic information. I feel keenly and strongly that the minister and the government will make a serious mistake and will be looked upon as interfering with something touching human rights and fundamental freedoms if this debate is denied. Many members of the house have exhausted their right to speak in the debate on the speech from the throne and they may be vitally interested in speaking. I refer to such members as my friend the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw). I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this request is in order and that it should be allowed.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minisier of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I just add one word on the subject that the leader of the C.C.F. has mentioned, namely the attempt the other day to do what is being attempted today. I did not mention the matter at the time because of the answer which you gave to him. However, I want to stress what has always been the understanding of the house since I came here and, from what I can read, has been the understanding on all other occasions. On those occasions when we are in general debates, as on the address and the budget at least, if not others, and perhaps even motions to go into supply, if these particular items for discussion are before the house there is then an opportunity to debate any matter that any hon. member wishes to bring before the house. I admit that the question of
Immigration-C. G. Hanna relevancy sometimes enters into the matter with respect to a particular amendment. Nevertheless, I think it has been the ruling of every successive Speaker in this house that on those general occasions anything can be said by an hon. member and any particular matter can be debated. In other words, any person speaking this morning or this afternoon could advert to this subject and say what he wished with respect to what the government is doing. Since that is the case, I think the rule has always been interpreted in the matter of urgency with respect to a particular matter as a matter of urgency of debate. I am quite sure any member can take part this afternoon and speak on this subject. I feel that any other ruling by Your Honour, if I may say so with respect, would be almost a complete reversal of our previous understanding.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Before your decision is rendered, I should like to make a few observations on the argument advanced by the Minister of Finance. I thought the argument advanced by the Prime Minister was flimsy, but the flimsiest argument of all has been that put up by the Minister of Finance. Never has a debate on the speech from the throne or a budget debate been interrupted more often by the government itself than in the last few years. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) has said, a score of members on this side of the house had expressed their opinions on the speech from the throne before this matter arose. It is either a matter of urgency or it is not.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: National emergency?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: It may not be to you, but it is to a lot of people throughout this country. The national honour of this country is at stake.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Hon. members may laugh. You have a great country, but you like to keep it to yourself and just let in the persons you like. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration should make a decision on this subject. The hon. member for Kamloops is quite within his rights in raising the matter. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said, there are members who had exhausted their time on the speech from the throne before this emergency arose. The Prime Minister has chided the hon. member for Kamloops for obtaining information from the solicitor. If we in the official opposition did not obtain information from the press or from friends we would never get it because the government does not

Immigration-C. G. Hanna give us information. Never since confederation has there been a government that has hidden the facts more than this government has. All the way down the line there has been excuse after excuse. What have you to hide?
Why does the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration sit so smug and look so pale when he fears this matter is coming before parliament? Tell us why. It is either a matter of urgency or it is not. If you and I, Mr. Speaker, were in Mr. Hanna's place- God forbid we should be-we have both been embarrassed before but not to that extent-*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have heard the serious remarks made by various hon. members. One of these days I will suggest that standing order No. 26 be amended so that it will leave the entire responsibility for the decision as to urgency in the hands of the house and not put it upon one individual, namely the Speaker. Some hon. members have stressed the fact that the purpose of standing order No. 26 is to have decisions taken. My own interpretation of standing order No. 26 is that it is the one which replaced the old motion for adjournment which was moved in the middle of a debate whenever some member wanted to discuss a matter which had nothing to do with the motion proposed at the beginning of a sitting. Those who have read the old debates will recall that as a debate was proceeding on a certain specific motion and a member would go beyond the field of relevancy of that motion, someone would say you need a motion for adjournment. He would stand up and move it, and the hon. gentleman who had the floor could carry on speaking about a subject which had nothing to do with the motion which had been the subject of discussion at the beginning of that debate. Therefore, because of the abuses brought about by this system, they brought in standing order 26, which used to be standing order 31.


This house now has a vehicle to discuss matters of actuality, some things that arise which hon. members feel should be debated. The net result of it is after the debate has taken place and is concluded the house has to adjourn. It is not a substantive motion although it has been amended once; but the amendment was not voted on. At the end of the sitting the adjournment takes place.
Here is my difficulty. Hon. members will agree that whenever there was a motion to go into supply in the offing or a motion to go into ways and means-they were debatable in sessions prior to last session- whenever the debate on the budget was currently going on, whenever the address in reply was currently going on, I do not think any hon. members can state one specific case where a motion under standing order 26 has ever been allowed by my predecessors or by myself. If there is one I would like to have it cited to me.
The other day when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar moved this type of motion it was a matter of great importance. I then told him that since we were entering the debate, if the Minister of Finance or any other minister had, under standing order 38(2), stood up on the first day or the second day and said, "Well, tomorrow we shall take up some other business", thereby postponing the continuance of the debate on the address to three, four, five or six days later than the next day-this is what I said on January 9, 1957, as recorded at page 23 of Hansard:
I do not say that he should not be permitted to make his motion again.
I would have allowed the hon. gentleman's motion the following day if the minister on the eve of that day had announced by virtue of standing order 38(2) that he would postpone the debate on the address. Since that did not occur, and we were carrying on the debate on the address, full opportunity was given for a debate on the matter of urgency which was contained in the motion of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
We have two more days for the debate on the address. Some hon. members claim they have exhausted their right to speak. Well, I have the list here before me of those who have spoken on the amendment, the subamendment and the main motion and there is no doubt that there is still a great deal of freedom for the purpose of discussing this matter.
Something has been said about obtaining information. Information may be obtained at question time. As a matter of fact I:

think the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saa-nich (Mr. Pearkes) asked some questions of the minister yesterday and the day before. The Leader of the Opposition has done so as well.
Now, if I do depart today from the previous practice of not allowing a motion under standing order 26 when the debate on the address is currently going on or a similar debate which affords great latitude I will not have justification for having refused the motion' made the other day by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. What would prevent us from having a motion tomorrow on a subject which may be different? I have to oppose my own personal opinion as to the urgency of debate in this case but standing order 26 is so construed as to leave that responsibility upon myself. Because of the past practice, as I say, of previous Speakers and because of my own' previous rulings 1 regret that I cannot accept the motion.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, may I point out that you have dealt with one matter of urgency, but is there not another matter of urgency before this house? This house has knowledge that a minister is proposing to take action which would defeat the course of justice. Do we have to sit here-

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I rise on a question of
personal privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Order. There has been a
question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Greenwood and the minister wishes to rise on a question of privilege himself. I think that we ought to rally ourselves around the decision which I have just made. It may not be a decision which is satisfactory, but nevertheless it is one which I feel I have to make. It may be much more painful to myself perhaps than to any other members in this house. However, I feel that I should not depart from the previous practice which has been established over a period of many years. One of these days I may depart from it, but when I do I wish to be sure that I have had full opportunity to study the implications of a change in the practice.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if this comes to a vote-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: IMMIGRATION
subsubtopic: C. G. HANNA    MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, will the Prime Minister give the
Inquiries of the Ministry house assurance that Christian G. Hanna will not be deported from Canada until after the date of the application for the hearing of the writ which I understand is on February 1.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot give any other assurance than the assurance that there will be no departure from the law established by parliament and that every opportunity for the consideration of what should be the proper application of that law will be given.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that undertaking does not go anywhere at all. I wish to ask the Prime Minister-

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Question.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: There is an application before the court, according to-

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: -the information I have. Will the Prime Minister give the undertaking that, until the courts decide, arbitrary practices will be discontinued in this case and this man will not be spirited out of the country so that he will be gone in any event and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration will be victorious.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
There will be no arbitrary action. The hon. gentleman overlooks, or perhaps does not overlook, the fact that this man could not be deported otherwise than by being placed back on the ship from which he disembarked. I do not know what procedures we could take to hold that ship pending a decision by the courts as to whether or not the man could remain in Canada. I do not know what the facts are.
The hon. member for Kamloops has suggested that the ship is going to depart from Canada this evening. It may very well be that advantage is attempted to be taken of the fact that if the ship gets away without this man, whether the courts decide he can stay in Canada or not, there would be no physical possibility of having him leave Canada because I understand the ship has already visited many ports and at each one there has been a refusal to allow him to land because of the fact that he is not one who could be admitted according to the entry laws of the countries of those various ports.
There is no desire to spirit him away. There is no greater obligation on Canada to take this man who apparently asserts that he was born at sea. I do not know on what ship or under which flag he says he was born. That seems to be the difficulty. I personally have not gone into the facts of this case, but I have been told that there

Inquiries of the Ministry are no special grounds for the recommendation that he should be admitted into Canada except the ground that nobody else wants to take him in anywhere else. It may be that we have more vacant space in this country than in most other countries; it may be that could be urged as a reason why we should do what nobody else wants to do; but these are matters which I do not think should become a contest between political parties.
There can be varying views as to whether we should in this country take on that which nobody else wishes to have elsewhere. That may be the opinion of some but it would not be the opinion of all, I am quite sure, because this parliament has enacted immigration legislation. If the legislation were to be wide open and everybody who could put his foot on Canadian soil would be entitled to stay here because that had happened, then there would be no need for that legislation. I am sure that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is giving and has given consideration to all the alleged facts.
However, I have not personally gone into those facts and there certainly will be no attempt to spirit him away in order to avoid the consequences of any court decision. On the other hand, there should not be the sanction by opinion of hon. members of this house to the effect that he will have to stay here because the only place where he could have been put back would be no longer in Canadian waters. That is a consideration which must have some bearing on the proceedings and I would like to know, if the hon. member for Kamloops does know, whether or not there has been an application to the supreme court of British Columbia as was announced over the radio this morning.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Prime Minister, since I must do this by way of a question, if he is aware that the objection taken is not to the refusal to admit this man but that the refusal was based on an improper hearing which was not a hearing at all? No one is alleging, now, that the man is entitled to remain permanently; what is being alleged is that he is entitled to a proper hearing to determine whether or not he is admissible, and it is to determine that issue that an application for a writ of certiorari has been made. The application is returnable on the 1st of February, and the assurance asked for is that the man would remain in Canada until then so that the finding of the court on the 1st of February would have some effect with respect to his right of a hearing as to his admissibility.
I would therefore like to ask the Prime Minister a further question. Can he say


whether, if, as I understand, assurances have been given that even though the ship may have left Canadian waters in the meantime, should Mr. Hanna be here and found to be non-admissible by judicial process, he will be returned at no cost to the ship, the right hon. gentleman would give an assurance in turn that this man will not be sent out of Canada before the courts can deal with his application?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman has different views, but I do not see how any arrangement could be made to return that man to the ship if the ship were not in Canadian waters.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: He could be sent on another ship.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: We might perhaps charter a ship to go and meet the other ship in some port, but I do not think that is a proper procedure to suggest.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: The Prime Minister has misunderstood my question; I would hesitate to suggest he has done so deliberately. Can he say whether if an assurance has been given, as I understand it has been given to the immigration officials of Vancouver, that if Hanna should be found to be nonadmissible then those interested in his application will see that he is returned to the ship at their expense, wherever it may be-they do not need to charter a ship to do that either-whether, if that undertaking has been given, it is not fair and reasonable to ask that the other undertaking I have mentioned should also be given?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: If that kind of undertaking were given by persons who are interested in this case and who are in a position to implement that undertaking, it would be a matter which should receive serious consideration, but the first appearance would be that efforts are being made to keep this man in Canada by one means or another until there would be no possibility of his not remaining in Canada no matter what the findings of the court might be.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
May
I address a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration? Does the minister consider that we in Canada have less of an obligation to admit this man than we had, some years ago, to admit a United States citizen with a criminal record who entered the country illegally, committed a crime after he had entered and was nevertheless allowed to remain here as a landed immigrant by virtue of an order in council?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: I do not suppose, Mr. Speaker, that that rhetorical question was meant to be answered at all, but on the assumption that possibly it was, I would say, as I said the other day, that I can find no ground under the law which would permit the minister or any of his officials to admit this man to Canada at all. That is under the law made by this parliament.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Why wouldn't you give him a proper hearing?

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would just possess himself in peace till I have finished I would be delighted to answer his question. As I said, no one has been able to find any ground on which this man could satisfy the requirements of the immigration law, but I am told by my department since this debate began in the house that we have information that a summons has been served on the chief immigration officer in British Columbia. That means that this case is definitely before the courts, and therefore I do not think it would be proper for me to say anything further about it.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Will the minister give the house an assurance that this summons having been served and the matter being sub judice his department will regard itself as legally bound to take no steps in this matter until the question is disposed of, and undertake not to return Hanna to the ship?

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: I will not give the house any legal opinion whatsoever.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Will the minister assure the house that he will abide by the law? No one has asked for a legal opinion.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Certainly, I will give an unqualified assurance that I will abide by the law.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Will the minister give an assurance that he will make no attempt to evade the consequences or the application of the law by having this man sent out of Canada before the law can be applied?

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: The minister's record is not a record of evasion at any time, and every hon. member of this house knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: That is an evasion in itself.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration if he would inform the house of the composition of the appeal board which heard this case?

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
I cannot do so offhand, but I will be glad to answer that question tomorrow.
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and a question of the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. The two questions are related. My first question is directed to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. If the ship sails tonight and takes Mr. Hanna, will the reference to the supreme court of British Columbia be proceeded with and a decision handed down?

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: I do not think that is a question that it would be in any way proper for me to answer, having regard to the fact that the case has already been taken before the courts. It is a hypothetical question in any case.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: My second question is directed to the Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Hanna case is apparently a case of a stateless person. Is there not some way of referring the case to some agency of the United Nations to deal with a matter of this kind so that this person will not have to be confined to a ship for the rest of his life? Is there anything we can do to have the reference made?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 assure my friend that I will be glad to give careful consideration to the implications of his question.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
May
I ask one question? Does not the United Nations rule apply only to people in refugee camps? If this man cannot get into a refugee camp to be treated as a stateless person, where is he to go?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: Statelessness is a problem that has been before the legal committee of the United Nations from time to time, but I would not want to give a ready answer to something to which I have not had a chance to give full consideration.

subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext: What I wanted to find out was whether or not, since Canada is now involved up to the ears in this whole matter, somebody in the government might not be prepared to refer it to some agency of the United Nations in order to get the problem solved. It is a humanitarian question and all of us ought to be concerned about it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: C. G. HANNA    REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT DEPORTATION WILL BE POSTPONED
speechtext:
I am sure the government is as concerned about it as anyone. My hon. friend will remember that Professor Humphrey, head of the human rights division of the United Nations, has already given some indication of interest in this matter, on behalf of the secretariat of the United Nations. However, I have not had a chance to really

Inquiries of the Ministry grasp the full implications of my hon. friend's question and I would not want to say any more now. I assure him the matter will be looked into, consistent with all the facts and our own obligations.

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL AGENCY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INTERNATIONAL AGENCY
subsubtopic: RATIFICATION OF STATUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, can the minister of external affairs say whether enough nations have as yet ratified the statute of the international atomic energy agency to make it operative? Second, is the government considering bringing forward a motion for ratification on the part of Canada before this session of parliament has come to a conclusion? I ask this question because of press reports of a discussion of a somewhat similar nature at the United Nations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Marlin (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL AGENCY
subsubtopic: RATIFICATION OF STATUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend was kind enough to give me notice of his intention to ask this question. In respect of the first part, my reply on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is that the international atomic energy agency will become operative when 18 of the signatory nations have deposited instruments of ratification. Among these 18 signatories must figure at least three of the following countries: France, United Kingdom, United States, the Soviet union, Canada. The United States, which is the depository government, has not advised us of the deposit of any instruments of ratification as yet. The government has no information that any of the signatories have as yet ratified the statute.
With respect to the second part of the question, as I indicated to my hon. friend before today's sitting, I am not in a position to give an answer. I have not yet had an opportunity on behalf of my colleague to discuss this matter with my colleagues. I shall ask that that part of the question be allowed to stand until I am in a position to give a definite reply.

subtopic: PILOT BOAT ACCIDENT, SAINT JOHN    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: PILOT BOAT ACCIDENT, SAINT JOHN    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext:
On Friday the hon. member for
Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) and yesterday the

hon. leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked whether it was my intention to order a public inquiry in connection with the loss of the pilot boat in Saint John harbour.
I should like to inform the house that I have now received the report of the preliminary investigation made by Captain Graves of my department, and that I am taking the steps necessary in order to hold a formal investigation pursuant to the Canada Shipping Act.

subtopic: PILOT BOAT ACCIDENT, SAINT JOHN    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: May I direct a question to the Minister of Transport arising out of the statement he has just made with respect to the public inquiry at Saint John and also with reference to my question on January 16 regarding that matter and also the department's responsibilities? Is the minister now prepared to say what immediate steps will be taken to replace the lost pilot vessel and what immediate precautions may be necessary to prevent in future any such sad accident?

subtopic: PILOT BOAT ACCIDENT, SAINT JOHN    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: In my understanding of the facts of the matter and of the shipping orders, there is no need for further precautions to be taken with regard to the operation of a pilot boat. With respect to the replacement of the pilot boat, I should like to tell the hon. gentleman that we are making arrangements to secure another and hope to have it available very shortly.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace):
subtopic: PILOT BOAT ACCIDENT, SAINT JOHN    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: Will the Minister of Transport inform the house why members of the families of those lost on the vessel in the pilot service at Saint John were denied counsel at the preliminary closed hearing while the steamship company was represented by counsel, lawyer J. Paul Barry?

subtopic: PILOT BOAT ACCIDENT, SAINT JOHN    STATEMENT ON REQUEST FOR PUBLIC INQUIRY
speechtext: The purpose of the inquiry which was held in Saint John was purely and simply to determine what were the facts of the accident in order that it would be possible to decide whether or not a public inquiry should be held. I believe that counsel representing the pilots was present and I believe one other counsel was present, although I do not know whom he represented. But it was not a'public inquiry. It was not an inquiry for the purpose of determining responsibility or guilt, and in point of fact there was no reason why anybody should have been represented at that inquiry.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON ABANDONMENT OF NEW YORK CENTRAL RAILWAY LINE, CORNW ALL-OTTAWA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ABANDONMENT OF NEW YORK CENTRAL RAILWAY LINE, CORNW ALL-OTTAWA
speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Lavigne) asked if consideration had been given to the question of transportation services to the municipalities affected by the abandonment of the New York Central line between Ottawa and Cornwall.
I find that by its order No. 90648, dated January 10, 1957, the board of transport commissioners on the application of the New York Central Railroad Company approved the abandonment of the line between Ottawa and Cornwall, provided that the abandonment would not take place earlier than February 15, 1957. This application was considered by the board at a public hearing held in Ottawa on December 12, 1956, at which interested parties were present or represented. In its judgment the board quotes textually the statement made at the public hearing by counsel for the railway company, which reads as follows:
No provincial highway runs directly through the territory of the line, but the district and communities in question are well served by adequate all-weather roads which connect with provincial highway No. 31 which runs from Ottawa to Morrisburg and there meets provincial highway No. 2 to Cornwall. Daily truck service is provided between Cornwall and the villages of Crysler, Newington, Finch and Ottawa. Berwick is served by Taggart Trucking of Ottawa, Ontario, and Glengarry Transport of Alexandria. Crysler, Russell and Embrun are served by Taggart Trucking and Glengarry Transport. Crysler, Berwick, Newington, Finch and Cornwall are also served by Earner Daye Transport Ltd. of Cornwall.
The judgment also notes that the freight handled on the line was negligible and, as the hon. member knows, there has been no passenger service on the line since the spring of 1954.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS MINIMUM PENSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Marler (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS MINIMUM PENSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) asked if since the end of the regular session of last year I had received representations on behalf of the retired employees of the Canadian National Railways in receipt of pensions of $25 per month for an increase in the amount of the pension. The answer to that question is that I have received no such representations. The hon. member also asked if further consideration has been given to this
Inquiries of the Ministry matter or if it will be given by the minister or the government. Representations were made recently to the management of the Canadian National Railways that any smaller pension now payable by it should be increased to $60 per month, but no action has been taken and the matter has not been considered by the Minister of Transport or the government itself.

subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Are press reports correct that the government of Manitoba has offered to come into the federal government's health or hospital insurance plan provided coverage is extended to include cases of mental illness and tuberculosis?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the press reports to which my hon. friend directs my attention. I would want to see them first.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: May I ask the minister a supplementary question? Can he say whether the government is considering extending the coverage provided in its plan so as to encourage more provinces to agree to it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: The government has not considered any modification in that particular or in any other particular. The proposal made by the federal government was a generous and comprehensive proposal, as was formerly acknowledged by the hon. gentleman. The government does not intend to include patients in tuberculosis and mental hospitals within the compass of its proposals for the simple reason that these are responsibilities now assumed by the provinces. In that particular we are following precisely the practice followed under the hospital insurance acts of Saskatchewan and British Columbia. With regard to tubercular and mental patients who receive treatment for their illness in general hospitals, they are included within the terms of the federal proposal.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: May I ask a further supplementary question? Is the government afraid that by amending its proposals six provinces might agree and the federal government would then have to deliver the goods with respect to health insurance?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, the government is not afraid. My hon. friend's persistence in asking these questions reminds me,

Inquiries of the Ministry as I told him on another occasion, of a cheer leader who considers that every time a touchdown is scored he is the one who has scored the touchdown.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: You are in a position to score.

subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext:
May I
ask a supplementary question? With respect to the offer made by the government to which the minister has referred, does the government propose to bring that offer to parliament to get the authority to make it and, if so, when?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: My hon. friend possibly has forgotten the terms of the proposal itself. The proposal contained a number of offers and with respect to those offers the federal government said that when six provinces representing a majority of the people of Canada had expressed their concurrence the federal government would take the necessary legislative steps to carry out its end of the matter. The federal government is not in any way retreating from these proposals. It stands by these proposals. When six provinces representing a majority of the people express their readiness to proceed, the federal government will act in accordance with the proposal it made last January as announced by the Prime Minister in the house and by myself when we were meeting with the provinces in another room in this building.

subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: Perhaps I understand the offer better than the minister understood my question. I asked the minister whether or not the government proposed to ask parliament for authority to make any such offers to the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: I cannot say any more than what I have said. I think if my hon. friend reads what I have said he will find that the question has been amply answered.

subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: The question is not answered. Another evasion.

subtopic: REPORTED MODIFICATION OF FEDERAL PROPOSALS
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Would the minister indicate what provinces have accepted the proposal and whether any of the provinces with Liberal governments have accepted the proposal?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
