speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house came very near missing the pleasure-or misfortune-of hearing me deal with a matter which, in the circumstances, should not be discussed at all in this house. I do not know the gentleman in question, nor am I acquainted with the facts which prevent him from entering Canada. One thing I do know, however, is that, as was stated on the other side of the house, the honour of our country is at stake. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the honour of six or seven countries is at stake, considering that those countries, for reasons unknown to me, refused to admit this man. I have always understood, even though I am not overly conversant with the rules of the house, that no question which is still sub judice can be discussed in the house. Though you do not need my official approval, Mr. Speaker, I might say that I fully share the opinion you expressed a moment ago and which, in the present circumstances, is certainly the most appropriate.
I would now like to continue the few remarks which I had intended to make with regard to the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
1 was dealing with the government's decision to establish a Canada Council for the encouragement of the arts, humanities and social sciences. I will dwell at length on this topic. It goes without saying that I do not intend to launch here into a detailed study of the matter, especially since my time is limited. Besides, I do not claim to have sufficient knowledge of all matters relating to the arts to justify my dealing with them at great
The Address-Mr. Dupuis length. However, I am sure that our artists will derive much benefit from the study which is to be made of the situation of the arts in this country. It should make for considerable progress in this field, it should allow our great Canadian artists to attain a very high standing in the fields of music, drama, motion pictures and others.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I said that, like most Canadians, I am sure, I am appreciative of the legislation the government intends to submit to the house at this session, more particularly with regard to the increase in university grants.
Again because I have but little time at my disposal, I do not intend to take part in the controversy touched off by this liberality, this generosity on the part of the present government. On the other hand, it does appear evident, to me at least, that as regards provincial autonomy, the good faith of the government cannot be questioned. I am not aware that the universities which were able to accept those grants in the past have ever been obliged to change one solitary item in their curricula, to replace any professor or to make the smallest change in their educational system.
I take this opportunity of repeating here that I would support no political party whatever which would attempt to infringe on the autonomy of any province; I will go further and say that I would fight it with all my strength. The provinces enjoy certain rights which have been guaranteed by confederation. We want every one of them to be perfectly free to exercise those rights. I repeat that no government, no political party, will ever have my support, or that of most members of this house, if it were to infringe upon provincial autonomy.
This year the government proposes to increase grants to provincial governments, to help technical and vocational training in schools under their immediate jurisdiction. No one, I believe, sounded the alarm in the name of autonomy because of the acceptance of this money which contributed to the equipment and in many other ways to the teaching given in those institutions. So far no one has refused, neither in wartime nor since the end of the war, the grants paid to technical schools for the training of tradesmen who wanted to increase their knowledge in the various trades.
I also congratulate the government upon the establishment of a Senate committee to study the means of improving the use of lands for agricultural purposes in order to

The Address-Mr. Dupuis contribute more efficiently to the expansion of agricultural production and of the income of those engaged in agriculture. We should not be surprised at that proposal.
There are two classes of people for which the government, and more particularly the Liberal party, has done something. I am thinking of the working class and the agricultural class, so that this decision comes as no surprise to me.
The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) pointed out that we are not holding aloof from agriculture. He quoted figures showing the considerable expansion shown by agriculture in the past three or four years. Moreover, the price support of butter, which enables producers to sell that commodity at a reasonable price, is already evidence that the agricultural class is receiving particular consideration from this government. The government continues to prove it by entrusting the Senate with a special study designed to determine how best we can help farmers to develop the land, especially submarginal land.
As far as we, city dwellers, are concerned, we are equally grateful, as municipal authorities are bound to be also for the decision made by this government to submit to this house at this session a bill to amend and extend the scope of the Municipal Grants Act, with a view to authorizing the payment of grants in lieu of taxes on federal property in all municipalities where such property receives normal municipal services.
By this measure, the federal government proposes to give more to the municipalities, thus making it easier for them to solve some of their problems. No one will accuse this government of infringing upon the autonomy of municipalities because it helps them financially.
It is true also that this government has been thinking about all classes of society, as can be seen from the proposals to be made to this house. For instance, it proposes to improve again the situation of merchant seamen, of wheat producers and of people who depend on the production of furs in the far north. In the speech from the throne, several other advantageous measures are mentioned, to wit:
Amendments of detail to a number of other acts will also be introduced.
Well, that opens the door to possibly a considerable number of sound and wise measures such as were always submitted by
fMr. Dupuis.]
this government, and by the Liberal party, possibly to correct certain wrongs or at last to increase the benefits granted by these various acts now in effect.
Aware of all these achievements of the Liberal party, of everything that we have done in the past and of what probably will be done-even though I do not know exactly what parliament will do at this session-and, taking into account the legislation that will be enacted as well as all previous achievements, we are not afraid to face public opinion.
The other day I heard the leader of the opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker)-I wish to congratulate him for his nomination to that post even though his electoral prospects may not be very bright, not so much because of himself personally but because of the backward policies of the party he is leading-move an amendment in which he said that public opinion has turned against us and that the majority of Canadians will vote against this government at the next election. I wonder if the people of Canada will support a conservative program which does not contain a single constructive item. Will they hesitate to make a choice between a government which has brought prosperity to this country and another party-I mean the Conservative party-under whose regime we have known failure, hardship, depression and unemployment.
We are not surprised either by the generous attitude of this government towards Hungarian refugees. It has understood that charity knows no frontier, and has practised it wherever possible. When the fate of human beings is at stake, the Liberal party and this government have shown their eagerness to relieve the burden of the victims of pitiful situations such as the one experienced recently by Hungarians.
Canada also largely contributed financially to the Colombo plan, and she has given substantial assistance to all the distressed countries in the world. This is something we can be proud of. I do not think that anybody on the other side of the house could reproach us with what we have done in this field, and I do not believe that any well-meaning citizen could blame us for the assistance we have given to those various countries which know nothing but extreme poverty, and disasters of all kinds.
Nevertheless, while fully endorsing the many steps taken by this government to help

other countries, I think that now, as we have always done, we should more than ever welcome the requests which are now made by a large number of our citizens who in the past, have served our country, have contributed to its progress, and I mean particularly our needy older people. We have been told about a surplus of hundreds of millions, and we are shown that the future holds the promise of an expansion still greater than in the past. I feel therefore that the government should give serious consideration to the request which is now addressed to them by a large number of citizens, by the various members of all parties sitting in this house, with whom I join, to increase substantially the pension now being paid to our old people.
I wonder if it would not also be time to study thoroughly the matter of the help and assistance which should be given to that class of people who have passed 60 years of age. Because, as everyone knows, it is very hard for a man of 40, and even more so for a man of 50, to get a new job when he has lost the one he had. The economic pattern has changed. The days are no more when a man of 50 could actually get employment, when his services were required because of his experience. Nowadays things are different; it is quite a problem for a man of 50 or more to find a job. Therefore it seems to me that, in view of existing conditions, of the difficulties besetting the middle-aged worker when he is looking for an occupation yielding enough to live on, and considering this country's era of prosperity, it might be proper to amend the present act so as to grant our elderly people a pension when they are 60. Well, I shall be told, this will will cost additional millions of dollars. I am not blaming this government. It was this government, this party, which initiated all the social legislation from which the nation benefits, in spite of opposition from the other side of the house, and more particularly on the part of the Conservatives who thought family allowances absolutely anti social and opposed or tried to obstruct the passing of the old age pension; and lastly, every social security legislation we introduced was at first attacked by the party which today, with elections in the offing, want it improved.
I know that the present government and all successive Liberal administrations have given our people all they could. We also know that this government will put at our
The Address-Mr. Dupuis disposal all improvements we have the right to expect for those who are obliged to rely on these allowances. I am not finding fault with anybody but it seems to me that certain requests which are being made should be granted, taking into account-in the light of the forecasts of the author of the Gordon plan and of the great American economists, as well as those of our own prominent businessmen in the country-that we may be on the threshold of a decade of continued increased prosperity, and it is during such a period that we ought to help our people.
No doubt that this government will agree to increase old age pensions and, at the same time, family allowances. There is no need to tell you that heads of families could put those increases to good use by giving an education to their children and meeting certain family needs.
I am no prophet but I am optimistic enough to think that this government, when the next budget is brought down, will give us, not so much a surprise-for we are so used to fine gestures on their part-but, at all events, great pleasure by granting those requests which are being made to them by people in various parts of the country.
I would like now to touch lightly on the question of bilingualism, which has been brought before this house. I have no time to discuss all its implications and all its details, but, nevertheless, we will unquestionably have to recognize that there is a French achievement in Canada and that French is going to be spoken more and more.
It will be claimed in some quarters that that may be the cause of misunderstanding, of national disunity. Far from it. There are other countries with two official languages. In another country, Belgium, even three languages, Flemish, Walloon and French, are used to about the same extent. I do not think that Flemish seeks to dominate Walloon or that Walloon tries to displace French.
We are not interested in gaining the upper hand over those who speak only English. There is no question of our imposing French upon our English-speaking fellow citizens or upon those who speak nothing but English. The French language is not imposed, it asserts itself, for it is one of the two universal languages. For instance, a man who comes from any country, providing he speaks French and English, is sure to be understood all over the world. There is, therefore, no question, I repeat, of imposing French, because French

The Address-Mr. Dupuis asserts itself. But it should be understood that when France lost her colony in 1763, our forefathers, the pioneers of this land, fought to preserve their language and that we also are determined to defend it against all attacks.
But I would point out to my English-speaking fellow citizens that from the standpoints of industry, trade, personal advancement and even of the exchanges they may have with other countries, it is in their own interest to know both languages. Once those who are particularly opposed to our language understand that it is in their own interest to speak French-even though they may not care to do so through sentiment-if they are realistic and I believe they are, they will come to speak both languages, and this will be of great help to them in business as well as in their relations with individuals of Canada and elsewhere.
In concluding my remarks on that subject may I assure those who might entertain some doubts on that point that nobody in the province of Quebec, where most Frenchspeaking Canadians are to be found, wants to hurt or to offend the feelings of those who do not speak our tongue. We want that clearly understood. I repeat that we want them to consider that it is in their own interest to speak French just as it is in our own interest to speak English. When they come to realize that this country is and will remain a bilingual country, we will have complete national unity. We will then be able to call ourselves Canadians from one end of the country to the other and we will be proud to speak both languages outside our country, to speak the languages of the pioneers, the language of the people who founded this country and the language of the people who gave it such an extraordinary economic development, I mean the English people and the French people, who kept on living and increasing in numbers in Canada.
A speech from the member for St. Mary would not be complete without a word about the Jacques Cartier bridge. Apparently I did not get the results I had expected, and that is why I again make to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) a request I have made time and time again, the abolition of tolls on that bridge. It is said that it cannot be done, in view of the fabulous sum of money derived from that source and the large expenses which are expected to be made. Besides, the consent of the provincial authorities would be required, and no request to that effect has
'Mr. Dupuis.]
been received so far from the provincial government, while the city of Montreal, which is the third party, has not yet expressed an official opinion on the matter. Therefore it might be difficult to get these tolls abolished before the three parties concerned come to an agreement. However something might be done for those who use that road, which should not be the responsibility of the federal government, as it comes under the municipal and provincial jurisdictions. That road serves a thickly populated area, if we take into account the thousands of people who live on the south shore. In the interest of those who come from Montreal and who have to cross to the south shore, because of this huge population, I believe that we should at least agree to abolish the toll now charged to the passengers in the various vehicles, and private cars. This would relieve to that extent the budget of workers, especially the thousands who are employed in Montreal. This would be only fair to the users of that bridge, and even to visiting strangers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it has been the age-old custom on the part of members of this house, I also wish to express my congratulations to the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) on their remarks and their contribution in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Considering the emptiness of the speech from the throne I feel they have done a very fine job in making something out of practically nothing. As it also has been the custom for members when speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne to bring to the attention of this house matters concerning their own particular constituency,
I intend also to direct part of my remarks to my constituency.
It has been a great privilege for me to represent the historic riding of Elgin since March 22, 1954. This constituency received
its name from a former governor general of Canada, Earl Elgin. As I have pointed out before to members in this chamber, my constituency is approximately 50 per cent urban and 50 per cent rural, with the city of St. Thomas being the major urban centre. St. Thomas for many years was and is still known as the railroad city of Canada. It was and still is to my knowledge the only city in Canada which has six railroads running through it. Due to many changes in railroading during the past number of years the railroad repair shops in this city have practically disappeared and at the present time they are almost non-existent. During this change in railroading many former employees of the railroad shops have had to seek employment elsewhere. Due to our city council who had a vision to the future and progressive boards of trade headed by one of the top industrial commissioners in Canada, St. Thomas has been able to offset this change in industrial employment by attracting a large number of industries and many United States subsidiary firms.
To attract this type of industry a city must have among other things adequate housing accommodation. The city of St. Thomas never has gone all out in a large scale housing program at any time. However, it has endeavoured to provide housing accommodation to meet the demands of industry as industry required housing. In April 1956 the city made application to have erected some 35 rental housing units. This application was made to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and at that time a survey was made in the city of St. Thomas to determine the needs. It was shown that the needs were definite at the time of the original application. Mr. Speaker, it took from April last year until the first part of January this year to obtain the final approval from the Department of Public Works and from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. This means that it will be well on in the summer months before the housing units can be completed to the point where they can be occupied. It would appear to me that a project of this kind could have been processed in much less time and in fact could have been processed in time to give much needed employment to our local contractors during the slack winter months.
I am sure that the people of the city of St. Thomas and of the surrounding area are at last, after having received promises over a period of ten years, pleased to see the start of construction on the new federal building. There are many people who may regret to see that the old landmark of the present

The Address-Mr. McBain post office is being razed. However, we anticipate that the new building will bring beauty along with additional accommodation to the city and the surrounding area.
In offering suggestions to the Department of Public Works there are two more on which I wish to comment at this time. One is the method employed in letting the smaller public works contracts. I am speaking of contracts in the range of from $1,000 to $10,000. I have been given to understand that the method used is to ask at least two contractors to submit a price on the project. Then what usually happens is that these two contractors get their heads together and they both bid on the project. Possibly one says to the other, "I had the last public works contract, I am busy now, you take this one, and I will make my tender a little higher." If this method were practised generally all across Canada the cost to Canadian taxpayers would be many thousands of dollars. It would cost them much more than if these small projects were locally advertised and the local contractors given equal opportunity to bid on the contracts on a competitive basis.
Mr. Speaker, I am not suggesting that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) himself is guilty of party patronage in letting these contracts. I know through my direct dealings with him that he is sincerely endeavouring to run his department on a nonpartisan basis. For the major public works needs those needs are considered on a merit basis, but when this authority is delegated to someone else down the party line it gets out of hand and some place, somewhere, somebody plays favouritism at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer.
My second suggestion to the Minister of Public Works is in connection with the letting of dredging contracts for the harbours of Port Stanley and Port Burwell. These two ports usually silt very badly during the winter and early spring, and on many occasions shipping is delayed for many days on the opening of the navigation season. The shipping is delayed because no contract has been let for harbour dredging and it is necessary to wait upon the Public Works Department to dredge a channel to let the boats come in. As this is an annual works project I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that contracts should be called earlier in the year so that the successful contractor would be in a position to start dredging as soon as the ice is out of the harbour.
In the 1955-56 season, when the dredging contracts were carried over, I believe there was less delay in spring dredging than in
[Mr. McBain.f
previous seasons when contracts were called for after spring soundings had been made and calculated.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to turn now to the subject of agriculture and bring to the attention of the house something of which we as agriculturists are very proud in our constituency.
I may say that Elgin county is proud of the fact that it has within its boundaries a cooperative that has expanded in recent years to be the largest farmer owned co-operative of its kind in Ontario and possibly in Canada. It was in 1944 that a number of progressive farmers in the county got behind the idea of a co-operative movement for the buying and selling of their grain crops, feeds, fertilizers, eggs, lumber and building supplies, fuel, etc.
In mentioning the distinction which has been gained through having the largest co-operative of its kind, I would point out the great importance of what its growth has meant to St. Thomas and Elgin county in services for and by the farmers. A business turnover of nearly $4J million each year for the last two years reflects the progress this industry has made. This growth can be translated into thousands and thousands of bushels of corn, soya beans, white beans, yellow eye beans, wheat, oats, barley seeds in variety, tens of thousands of tons of fertilizer and mixed feeds.
In 1955 over 900,000 bushels of corn were bought and sold through this co-op. This corn went mainly on the market as feed in competition with subsidized western feed grains. This co-operative is one of the few that returns all its patronage dividends to its farmer member shareholders as cash returns. In March of 1956, patronage dividends were returned to over 2,400 members to the amount of $88,000, and a total of over $500,000 has been returned as patronage dividends in 11 years of operation. This is a kind of farm service which has made Elgin Co-operative Services the largest farmer-owned buying and selling co-operative of its kind. With such a record of service its future would appear to be unlimited so long as Elgin county continues to have farmers and farm families of the type and calibre who have brought about this great development.
I bring this matter to the attention of this chamber and the government because I feel there are many other communities all across Canada which could benefit immensely by the government showing more initiative in lending support to assist co-operative organizations to become established on a sound financial basis. This would help in some measure to offset the increased cost of production.

I wish to turn now to another agricultural item which is very important in my riding, along the shores of lake Erie, and in other areas in Canada where people are able to grow tobacco. Tobacco is a very important item in the nation's economy at the present time. The Canadian government derives, on an average, $233 million a year in revenue from the industry if one includes property taxes, income taxes and excise tax on cigarettes, cigars and so on.
When cultivation of tobacco was first started in the early twenties, 1,000 acres was produced. The average yield per acre was 800 pounds. This has blossomed to an allocated acreage last year of 113,000 acres yielding between 160 and 170 million pounds with a market value around $70 million.
In keeping with this growth in the industry itself, the value of tobacco farm land has increased tremendously in recent years. Land which was worth between $30 and $40 an acre back in the twenties before tobacco was grown on it has increased in value in some areas to as much as $1,000 per acre. The increase in production which I have mentioned has also seen the average yield increase to about 1,400 pounds per acre. For the last two years the industry seems to have been undergoing a levelling-off process; the get-rich-quick day is gone. The price of land makes it unwise to invest between $100,000 and $150,000 in a first class tobacco farm, for it would take a lifetime to get the original investment back as things stand at present. Banking credit restrictions are "putting the squeeze" on the tobacco grower.
One thing that would improve the industry would be the lowering of the excise tax on cigarettes and other tobacco products. At the present time the farmer's return for every pack of cigarettes is about three cents. Manufacturers and distributors take about 12.5 cents and government revenues account for over 17.5 cents on every package selling to the consumer for 33 cents.
I wish to bring the attention of the house to the system under which tobacco is purchased at the present time. The tobacco market opens on a set day, but before that date the tobacco company graders have been to every tobacco farm and have looked over the tobacco each grower has to sell. The crops are graded, so the companies know exactly what tobacco is available before any pricesetting meeting takes place. Since these companies know what a grower has to sell, they set a price before the buyer drives up the farmer's lane. The buyer offers his price, take it or leave it. He could be on the farm less than 10 minutes and then is gone. There is no time for the grower to make up his 82715-33
The Address-Mr. McBain mind and no time to discuss what he himself thinks his crop is worth. If the grower wants an hour or so to think it over he stands to lose, for when the buyer returns he often offers from half a cent to three cents less than his original offer an hour before. No matter what happens, under the present setup the grower stands to lose.
I should like to read into the record a letter published in the Rodney Mercury of January 16, 1957. I believe the writer of the letter expresses the feelings of the many hundreds of flue-cured tobacco growers under the present system. The letter was addressed to the editor of the paper and the writer signs himself, "A New Canadian Grower". The letter reads:
In the past you showed great understanding of problems facing all the tobacco growers. Your editorials concerning tobacco buying practices were true voice of the growers. For this you deserve our sincere thanks. We hope in the future your paper will take the same stand in regard to our efforts to correct the present rotten situation.
I am positive the people who helped to organize the Ontario flue-cured tobacco marketing association had the best intentions to protect the rights of both growers and buying companies. Unfortunately, it turned out to be of great service to the buying companies in cheating the grower.
In our bylaws there are many restrictions, fines, obligations and fees imposed upon the grower members. Nothing of this kind is for the buyers. If there were any it would be disregarded by them anyway because they are the masters of the situation they created.
The present grading and buying practices turned into a shameless situation robbing the grower of his hard-earned profit. Humiliation of the grower by the buyers during so-called marketing time reached its peak. God help the farmer who dares to show his dissatisfaction about the cheating he gets or refuses to sell his crop for the price the first buyer offers.
No wonder the press representatives are not allowed to attend the meetings of the board. No wonder the grower members are kept in the dark in all the dealings of the board. No wonder the grower members are not informed about the findings of the federal government's investigation committee and its recommendations. Something is really wrong with the board.
I am a new Canadian and I work hard to earn my living. I do not enjoy too many of those long hours of hard work, as an Elgin tobacco grower stated a few weeks ago in his letter to the editor. I would rather be in some resort with our chairman of the association vacationing. Unfortunately, I consider hard work as my obligation to my family and the community I have chosen.
I believe the present situation in the marketing association would not exist if all the tobacco growers were Canadians of old standing, but I do not think only the new Canadians are to blame. In my opinion those of long standing should take the lead in correcting the present situation. I assure you new Canadians will gladly follow them. After all it would not be too polite for a new Canadian to reorganize in the country where he just warmed up his feet. Let's forget all the differences between us and unite in the efforts to do something about this association of ours.
Our hopes are raised by the suggestions of the federal government for the changes in marketing control: the recent secret meetings of the growers in various parts of the country and the news that

The Address-Mr. Kickham the petition asking the government to set up the marketing legislation will be circulated among us, are most welcome. I assure you my signature under this petition will be among thousands of others who feel that time has come for changes.
I would like to take this opportunity to ask the fellow growers to express their views in this paper. Let's write about our problem. Let's show the buyers how much we hate the present rotten business. I do not think they will be too happy reading it. And when the petition comes in to our district asking our government to step in, let's everyone sign it.
That letter is signed, as I said before, by "A New Canadian Grower". We know that the supreme court is still considering the merits of our farm products marketing act and as yet has not rendered its decision as to the validity of the act. Regardless of what the decision may be, I hope that the government, if it is still in power and not dissolved by that time, will give every assistance possible to the flue-cured tobacco growers to form a marketing association under farm products marketing legislation should they so wish and decide to do so.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. R. F. L. Hanna for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Shaw.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with hon. members who have preceded me in this debate in extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Hanna) and the seconder (Mr. Robichaud) for the [Mr. McBain.}
splendid contributions they have made in opening the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I wish first to express my thanks on behalf of the people of my county for the public works program carried on in my county and to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) for the new construction of the Georgetown railway wharf, and the construction of a new frost-proof potato warehouse on the wharf, replacing the now obsolete warehouse this coming season.
A great deal has been accomplished in the dredging of harbours, thus deepening the waterways to give sufficient draft for fishing boats to reach the wharves and also in new construction on breakwaters and wharves. All this work was necessary in order to assist fishermen and farmers in carrying on successfully their respective industries. There still remain numerous requests for similar work to be carried out at many fishing centres, and I am always fervently hoping and asking that those requests will be met through sufficient money appropriations. I realize, however, that we cannot expect to have everything done all at once, as a government can only spend money in keeping with their annual revenue from year to year. I can say to the minister that we are thankful for the recognition and the appreciation he has acknowledged of our need in regard to assisting fishermen and farmers in the prosecution of their daily pursuits.
Our farmers and fishermen suffer greatly because of the continuous freight rate tariff increases, and of course this applies to the four Atlantic provinces particularly because of our geographical location in Canada. Long hauls mean that we are without the truck transport competition enjoyed by the central provinces, with accompanying lower freight tariff rates to remedy this discrimination. I would suggest to the government that if they compensated the railways for the increases in freight tariff rates, amounting to over 100 per cent since 1945, especially on our major products such as coal, potatoes and fish, this action would assist the economy of the Atlantic provinces greatly.
As each of those three are bulky products and as the present freight rates bear heavily on those industries, I would also urge that the feed grain freight assistance as well as the Maritime Freight Rates Act be restored to its former effectiveness before the horizontal increase in freight rates took place. To my mind there is no better measure that the government could decide upon to assist the economy of the Atlantic provinces than to absorb a large portion of freight rate tariffs on our products going to central Canada. This

would give us the most direct and immediate relief and the greatest encouragement, and would be equal to a blood transfusion to our economy. The ever-increasing freight rates are a terrific burden on us and do not allow us to compete on equal terms.
It has been said that any depressed area in Canada reflects itself on the whole economy of Canada. I believe this statement to be true. I believe I have suggested one obvious way of mitigating our economic difficulties, at least to some extent.
Many farmers in our province in need of funds to finance their farm operations find it most difficult to procure a loan through the Canadian farm loan board because of the high level of security required before a loan is approved. The Canadian Farm Loan Act has been in operation for the past 27 years and provides for only 14 per cent of all farm loans in Canada. The losses sustained since its inception have been insignificant. To assist farmers in acquiring loans the security required should be reduced by 25 per cent. If this were done, many applicants who are now ineligible could become qualified and could take advantage of the interest rates and amortization provisions for which the act provides. A decrease in the amount of security required, in line with my suggestion, would permit greater latitude to be exercised by the district supervisors and would give the act more flexibility. At present it is far too restrictive in character. It would seem that the length of time which elapses from the date of application until appraisals are made on the farm properties is entirely too long. Apparently some district offices are understaffed and, through no fault of the district supervisor, the applicant becomes frustrated because of the extremely long waiting period.
This Canadian farm loan board could be made the best loan agency in Canada, but it must cast off much of its security requirements. I trust that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) will broaden out this legislation and make its lending facilities reach out to supply the borrowing needs of many more farmers than it does at the present time.
I should like to say a word on veterans pensions. Many veterans who served in the first world war but who did not go beyond England are not eligible for the war veterans allowance. The same thing applies in the second world war in respect of veterans who did not serve outside of Canada and Newfoundland. Some of those veterans voluntarily would have gone overseas but, because of special qualifications, they were retained in Canada. They are now denied war veterans allowance by our legislation.

My suggestion to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) is to grant to all veterans reaching the age of 60 years $40 per month, in the same way as all citizens reaching the age of 70 automatically receive $40 per month. Forty dollars per month should be of great assistance to many veterans who find themselves in distressing financial circumstances.
Our fishing industry is most important in my province. The provincial and federal departments concerned are co-operating in splendid work in research and applying scientific methods to the catching of fish and also to the manner of processing the fish.
I should like to see the cold storage and refrigeration legislation broadened so that packers and processors would become eligible to receive subsidies for the construction of refrigeration plants. Refrigeration is now an absolute necessity and if the packers and processors were given assistance they would be able to provide this necessity. Often they are unable to provide refrigeration out of their own resources, and any assistance granted is of benefit to each individual fisherman.
Before concluding my remarks I wish to thank the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) and his parliamentary assistant (Mr. Mac-Naught) for the splendid work they did at my request in allowing quahaugs to be removed from polluted waters in Queen's county, transferred to the beaches of King's county for cleansing purposes and reclaimed for processing in King's county. I am not going into detail about the difficulties the minister met, but I do know there were many barriers to hurdle because of health regulations both in Canada and the United States. In this respect we had the fullest co-operation from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I shall defer any further remarks on fisheries until the minister's estimates are before the committee.

speechtext:
am very happy to have the privilege of taking part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, particularly at the present time when I am given the opportunity of supporting the subamendment which was so capably presented to this house last Thursday by my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw). This subamendment criticized the government for failing to take effective action to stop the continuous rise in the cost of living; secondly, the failure of the government to lay down and follow policies under which the Canadian farmers and other primary producers can enjoy an equitable share of the prosperity

The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith which Canada can achieve; thirdly, the failure of the government to bring old age pensions and other social security payments into line with the present cost of living.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with a few of the many problems which are confronting men and women engaged in our basic industry, agriculture, and to suggest to the government a few steps which, if the government is truly interested in the wellbeing of this industry, can be taken to relieve the situation in which farmers across Canada now find themselves. Since coming down here we have been made very conscious of the fact we are going to ask the people across Canada very soon to again choose the government they wish to manage the affairs of our great country for another four or five years. Since that is the case, now is the time for each and every one of us in this house to do a little reflecting. We should ask ourselves a few very simple questions such as these: Have we in the past years done our best to serve our constituents and the people across Canada as they deserve to be served? Have we seen to it that all phases of our economy have been fairly treated or have we permitted some sectors of our economy to suffer?
As to the last question, Mr. Speaker, we in this group feel that many segments of our economy have been badly treated. It is interesting to read the glowing accounts of our national prosperity but it is very difficult to reconcile this rosy picture with the true state of affairs found in the agricultural industry, especially when we find approximately 18 per cent of the people who are engaged in agriculture in Canada receiving less than 7 per cent of the national income. However, we cannot find any evidence in the speech from the throne that it is the intention of the present government to do anything about this situation. It is true that this matter has been causing great concern throughout Canada. In fact, the supporters of the present government, the delegates who attended the Alberta Liberal association convention at Calgary in November of last year, expressed their dissatisfaction with the federal agriculture policy, if it could be called a policy, which has been followed over the years. According to press reports this convention asked for a system of parity prices on farm products, and also urged the government towards greater efforts to find markets for our grain and other agriculture products.
This convention passed a resolution urging the government to provide long-term loans to young farmers. Another resolution which was passed at this particular convention


deals with the equalization of floor prices for hogs as between the eastern and Pacific coast markets. I am given to understand that a good percentage of the delegates attending the convention represented the agriculture industry of Alberta and one delegate used these words in describing his position. "Farmers are clinched; they cannot move. The government tells us we are prospering but everyone is in debt." In order to prove my statement that these delegates who are supporting the Liberal party are concerned and are unhappy about the situation as it now exists may I cite the fact they said "that something must be done about agriculture policy if we wish to elect Liberal members in the west".
Now, Mr. Speaker, these requests I have mentioned have been a part of the agriculture program of the Social Credit party down through the years. Even though we have advocated these policies in this house, the government has not seen fit to do anything about them. Last summer, for example, to give you one illustration, we received the assurance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that after the end of the crop year, July 31, he would see to it that attempts would be made to ensure that those points in the west which were on a low quota basis would be given a preference in the new crop year. I wish to be fair in this matter. I do not wish to blame the Canadian wheat board at all for the chaotic conditions that exist in the marketing of wheat in the west. Even though the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is reported to have made this statement while attending a meeting in southern Alberta: that the Canadian wheat board was the sole control of the marketing of wheat I am not prepared to accept that statement. The Minister of Agriculture knows full well that the Canadian wheat board can market our wheat only within the confines of the faulty marketing policies of the present Liberal government and the financial policies adopted by the government as well.
Last summer we had the privilege of sitting in on the hearings of the agricultural committee at which the Canadian Pacific Railway was in attendance. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Pacific Railway must stand condemned for a part of the situation which now exists on the western prairies as far as grain marketing is concerned. I feel that the Canadian Pacific Railway deliberately failed to co-operate last spring with the then transport controller. I can find little evidence, Mr. Speaker, that the same railway has tried very seriously to do anything about relieving the

situation that is found on the Canadian Pacific lines in western Canada at the present time.
I have followed the marketing of grain in my riding very closely and I have found many points which were on a 5-bushel quota had not completed their 2-bushel quota at the end of the crop year, July 31, 1956. On the other hand, I know of points in western Canada which were on an 8-bushel quota on July 31 of last year and have now achieved a completed 3-bushel quota. I have been in constant touch with the Canadian wheat board with regard to this situation, since it affects farmers in my riding, and I just wish to read briefly from a letter which I received in November from a leading official of the Canadian wheat board. He had this to say:
I would point out that both railways have materially increased their car supply in the shipping of grain during the period from August 1 up to present. From August 1 to October 31, the C.P.R. has supplied 43,830 cars as compared to 28,415 last year; the C.N.R. has supplied 41,598 cars as compared to 29,278 last year. However, notwithstanding the fact that the C.P.R. have increased their supply by approximately 15,000, the C.N.R. have increased their cars by approximately 12,000, but the total number of cars supplied by each road is just about equal when you take into consideration that about 57 per cent of the grain that we have for shipment is located on the C.P.R., with about 43 per cent on the C.N.R. You will appreciate that, as long as the C.N.R. continues to match the C.P.R. supply the stations on the C.N.R. will be in better shape than those on the C.P.R.
In other words, just as long as this government refuses to appoint a new transport controller with the power to direct orderly and equitable marketing of grain in the west this situation will continue and the farmers living along the C.P.R. lines will continue to be discriminated against.
I know that some attempts have been made to justify this situation. Several reasons have been advanced. Most of the reasons which have been advanced have been decidedly weak. Perhaps one of the most prevalent reasons is the need of wheat of a particular quality; that shipping orders are given for a certain grade of wheat. That argument does not stand up when you look at two points not more than 10 miles apart. The wheat marketed at these two points is in most instances of the same quality and grade. Therefore, that argument must necessarily fall down.
In closing this matter, Mr. Speaker, may I say I do feel that the government should do something immediately to see that the Canadian Pacific Railway takes immediate steps to put into the west the same percentage of cars as the C.N.R. They should do something about trying to catch up with the manmade lapse of six weeks last spring. As I pointed out a moment or so ago, the situation
The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith
in the west continues to be serious. In the west low quotas mean that the farmers are unable to market their grain. It means that they are unable to get cash money to pay their taxes and to do other things. We are told that one of the reasons that there is such a glut of wheat in the west is that there is a surplus of grain throughout the world. At this time I wish to refer to a short article which is entitled, "How Big Is The Surplus?" It deals with the surplus of wheat as it exists in the world today and reads as follows:
The present large stocks of wheat are a serious impediment to the ready marketing of new production. They are regarded gloomily by governments, farmers and business people in the export countries. The Canadian Bank of Commerce recently termed the wheat carryover as "astronomical".
There is no doubt that under our pattern of trade and distribution the situation is serious but the volume is inclined to impress us beyond its real proportions. We see the 11 billion bushel world carryover as almost the equivalent to the entire normal export figure for a one and a-half year period.
We overlook the fact that the world's population is also astronomical. There are over 2J billion people and in terms of food reserves we have only 36 pounds of wheat per person. In the United States, where flour consumption is moderate, 190 pounds of wheat a year per person is consumed.
For much of the world population wheat is unobtainable but the annual consumption is in the neighbourhood of 6 billion bushels. A 11 billion bushel surplus is the equivalent to a three-months supply for this wheat-eating section.
Awkward as carryovers may be to world trade, a 90-day reserve supply of such an important food commodity does not seem unreasonable.
I say, Mr. Speaker, few livestock men would care to operate on a narrower basis as far as basic food reserves are concerned. The article goes on to say:
The human race should be able to design an economy that would permit it to carry some assurance against emergency food depletion without causing a marketing breakdown and penalizing the producer.
I mentioned a short while ago that 18 per cent of the people of Canada are engaged in the basic industry of agriculture and they receive less than 7 per cent of the national income. There are many reasons for this. Perhaps one of the reasons for the present condition in which farmers find themselves is that the farmers of Canada are perhaps the only major wheat exporting people in the world who are operating in a purely unprotected market as far as the selling of their products is concerned. The farmers of Canada are finding themselves entwined in a terrific cost-price squeeze. That is perhaps true to some extent of farmers throughout the whole world.
Here I have a short article which gives the over-all position of the farmers throughout some of the major countries of the world. I find that in the period from January 1, 1953 to the end of the first three months of

The Address-Mr. J. A. Smith 1956 the over-all position of the farmers in these countries followed a pattern. In Australia the over-all position of farmers declined 15 per cent; in Canada in that period the position of farmers declined 19 per cent; in Finland the over-all position was up 23 per cent; in West Germany, up 11 per cent; Japan, up 4 per cent; in the Netherlands down 5 per cent; and in the United States down 16 per cent.
I wish to point out that as far as the farmers in Canada are concerned their position declined 19 per cent, more than in any other country shown in this set of figures. This is a sad picture, but it is true. I have never heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) get up on the floor of this house and give a convincing argument against the statement that agriculture in Canada is in a deplorable condition. I am looking forward with interest to his doing so at some time during the present session. I would like to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) why he has permitted our basic industry to dip down to such low economic levels. This situation, if allowed to continue, will eventually lead to the complete collapse of our food producing industry. I know that in our own area local government bodies along with businessmen and others who are associated with the farmers are finding it increasingly difficult to carry on as a result of this ever-decreasing income.
In my own municipality of Vermilion river arrears of taxes have risen to the startling figure of $609,715. This means that 36 per cent of all the parcels of land in that municipal district are in arrears of taxes. In the municipal district of Wainwright, which is south of my municipality, a similar condition exists. Arrears of taxes in 1955 had accumulated in that municipality to $267,077 with 108 parcels of land under tax recovery.

speechtext:
Forget . about that. You do not know about that or you would not speak that way. The reason for the great increase in tax arrears in these two municipal districts must be obvious to all, even to my hon. friend the member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne). It simply means that the farmers of these districts do not have the cash with which to pay their taxes. I know of many farmers who for the first time since the depression years have had to forgo the payment of their annual taxes.
I now wish to spend a few moments on a matter which is of concern in this house. It is the unfairness of the present existing floor prices on hogs. When one considers that 90 per cent of the hogs exported from Alberta in 1955 found their way to markets
[Mr. Smith (Battle River-Camrose) .1

in British Columbia and that it costs only $1 per hundredweight to ship a hog from Edmonton to Vancouver, how can the Minister of Agriculture justify the wide spread in the floor prices on hogs that exists between the Edmonton and the eastern markets of Toronto and Montreal? The floor price for Edmonton is $18.50 per hundredweight and $23 per hundredweight on the Toronto-Montreal market. Surely if there is any justice at all in the differential of floor prices for hogs across Canada or any justice at all for this spread the minister would establish a floor of $22 per hundredweight on the Edmonton market.
The farmers of Alberta raise good hogs. They would raise more if they were assured of a fair return for their labours. The drastic reduction in the number of hogs raised in Alberta last year was a direct consequence of the unstable markets that existed the previous year. At one time Great Britain was a large importer of Canadian pork products, but for reasons best known to the present administration the market has presently disappeared.
I wish to go back to the year 1935 when this present administration took over. That year we exported to Great Britain over one million hogs. In 1940, just at the beginning of the war, we were exporting to Great Britain over 2,800,000 hogs. I am prepared to admit that during the war period there was some increase in the demand for Canadian hogs. At the end of 1945 we exported to Great Britain 3,600,000 hogs. By 1950, five years after the close of the war, the British market had slipped from a high of 3,600,000 to just slightly over 600,000 hogs. Five years later in 1955 we exported to Great Britain 53 hogs. Up until the end of July last year we had not sold Britain one pound of pork products. Surely there is something wrong with the marketing policies of a government which allows such a situation to develop.
I would like to comment briefly on the operation of the agricultural prices support board. The story has been spread across Canada that the operation of this board has cost the taxpayers of Canada a tremendous amount of money. The board was established in 1946. Since 1946 the administration of the agricultural prices support board has cost the people of Canada $89 million. The greatest part of this amount, $70 million, was spent in paying the loss to the farmers of Saskatchewan by reason of the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak in 1952.
The remainder over a ten-year period was allocated in this manner:	$8.5 million for
cost of butter support since 1949; $6.7 million

for apples; and $2 million for potatoes. The other support items are relatively small, not including the foot-and-mouth crisis. In the ten-year period price supports have cost the treasury of Canada less than $2 million per year or about 15 cents per person in Canada per year. That certainly is not an extravagant amount to guarantee to the farmers of Canada support prices.
I turn now to the figures of the bureau of statistics, using as a base the period 1943 to 1945. The estimated parity price on butter in 1956 is 71.6 cents per pound. The average marketing price of first grade butter during the past year was 58.6 cents. As far as hogs are concerned, using the same period, the average market price for B-l hogs across Canada was $25.98, parity $28.87 per cwt. Grade "A" (large) eggs, per dozen in Montreal parity 71.4 cents; the average market price only 58 cents.
I think, Mr. Speaker, it is high time the Minister of Agriculture gave serious consideration to bringing the Agricultural Prices Support Act in line with the parity established for the base period 1943-1945.
At the commencement of this address I suggested that I would request the government to give very serious consideration to certain proposals which I feel would help relieve the crushing burden now borne by Canadian agriculture. I would like to see the present government take immediate action with regard to certain proposals:
1.	A system of cash advances on farm-stored grain, payment of these advances to be administered by some agency other than the Canadian wheat board, and the cost of administration to be borne by the government.
2.	Immediate action to be taken toward the extension of permanent government-owned storage facilities and the renewal of the policy of encouraging the use of temporary off-site storage facilities to enable farmers to deliver their grain.
3.	Introduction of an aggressive and realistic foreign sales policy as far as our agricultural products are concerned.
4.	Opening of a thorough investigation into the merits of the two-price system of marketing our agricultural products with a view to establishing a parity price for all agricultural products.
5.	The marketing of flax and rye to be handled by the Canadian wheat board.
6.	Equalization of the floor prices paid on hogs all across Canada and a raising of these prices to bring them in line with estimated parity using the period 1943-1945 as the base period.
The Address-Mr. Robichaud
7.	Amendments to be introduced to the Farm Loan Act to make this act of some use to young men wishing to enter the agriculture industry.
8.	The enactment of an all-risk insurance plan which will assure the farmers of Canada a just income in case of crop failure or some other disaster.
9.	The acceptance of sterling and the currency of other lands to stimulate trade with those countries, and
10.	The immediate appointment of a transport controller with power to see that there is an equitable distribution of box cars in the west at all times.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the remarks of my colleague for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) and other members of this group in support of their plea for further assistance to the senior citizens of this country, and to make one observation concerning the C.P.R. strike.
This strike meant a nine-day delay with regard to the movement of grain along the C.P.R. lines. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) to use whatever influence they may have toward seeing that grain movement along the C.P.R. system be accelerated as much as possible so that farmers delivering grain at C.P.R. points will not have to suffer any more than necessary as a consequence of this strike.
